### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-02 19:50

Here's the full feature inventory of what you've actually got running.

## Platform & architecture
- NestJS modular monolith — clean module boundaries per domain, single deploy, ready to extract services later.
- PostgreSQL via TypeORM, migration-driven schema (12 migrations, no auto-sync), Redis for queues/cache, all in Docker for local dev.
- Two-role DB connection model: migrations/seed run as the owner; the app runs as a least-privileged role so security is actually enforced.

## Multi-tenancy & security
- Postgres Row-Level Security, forced on every tenant table, keyed off a per-request vendor GUC — isolation proven in both directions (scoped reads, cross-tenant writes rejected) under a non-superuser role.
- Per-request tenant context via AsyncLocalStorage + a transaction interceptor; a `TenantRunner` extends the same guarantee to background jobs and public webhooks.
- Passwordless OTP auth → JWT, role-based guards (`platform_admin`, `vendor_owner`, `property_manager`, `tenant`, `contractor`).
- Webhook HMAC-SHA256 signature verification (raw-body), global rate limiting, and API-key auth (SHA-256 hashed, prefix lookup) for machine-to-machine integrators.
- Append-only general ledger (DB-level UPDATE/DELETE blocked), segregated trust accounting, `SECURITY DEFINER` functions for the legitimate cross-tenant lookups (auth bootstrap, billing worklist, webhook/API-key resolution).

## Tenant lifecycle (the core loops)
- Properties → units → rooms hierarchy with a unit status engine.
- Listings + applicant funnel: create/publish a vacancy → public application → screening (income-to-rent + credit → recommend) → approve, which provisions the tenant user + membership, opens an active lease, and flips the unit to occupied.
- Leasing: fixed/month-to-month/co-living, tenant linkage.

## Financial engine
- Double-entry ledger with balance enforcement (validated in integer cents); corrections only via reversing entries.
- VAT-aware invoicing (ZA 15%) with atomic ledger posting; recurring monthly billing + daily dunning/late-fees via BullMQ.
- Payment collection & allocation (Stitch), idempotent initiate, webhook settlement clearing AR.
- Deposit trust accounting: capture into a segregated trust account, interest accrual owed to tenant (RHA), and inspection-driven move-out returns with lawful deductions.
- Owner statements + split payouts (Paystack) for the agency model, with owner-billable expense recovery folded in.
- Chart of accounts auto-provisioned per vendor.

## Operations & comms
- Inspections as structured data (move-in/out/periodic checklists, per-item deductions feeding deposit returns).
- Documents with presigned S3-style upload/download, versioning, role-based access scope, and webhook-driven e-signature.
- Async multi-channel notifications (push/SMS/email) with templates, per-user preferences, and quiet hours — wired to rent-issued, payment-received, and overdue events.
- Reporting: rent roll, arrears aging, collection rate/summary.

## Market/white-label layer
- Pluggable providers behind interfaces (payments, storage, e-sign, notification channels) — swap per market/environment without touching domain code.
- ZA policy pack: VAT, RHA deposit rules, PPRA (Fidelity Fund Certificate / trust-account gating) — rules in code, selection in vendor config.
- White-label branding via `Vendor.config` (colour, name — the tenant app already reads it).

## Frontends (live)
- Tenant mobile app (Expo/React Native): OTP login, rent dashboard, one-tap pay, lease view — running against the API.
- Web back-office (Next.js): manager dashboard (rent roll, arrears, collection, run-billing) + listings create/publish.

## Quality
- 15 unit-test suites / 54 tests covering all the pure logic (ledger, VAT, allocation, deposits, statements, screening, notifications, signatures, API keys, etc.), all green.

## Honest gaps (not built / stubbed)
- Maintenance/ticketing and internal messaging (comms) are backend stubs — the tenant app's "log ticket" is deliberately disabled.
- Providers are dev stubs (Stitch/Paystack/S3/DocuSign) — real credentials and SDK calls not wired.
- A couple of list-read endpoints are missing (`GET /owners`, `GET /listings/applications`), so the back-office doesn't yet have Owners or Applications pages.
- Landlord mobile app not built; tenant app doesn't auto-refresh paid status or view documents.
- No production concerns yet: CI/CD, Hetzner deployment, managed EU Postgres, Redis-backed rate-limit storage for multi-instance, observability/error tracking.

Want this as a Markdown file for the repo (e.g. `docs/STATUS.md`), or should I keep going on one of the gaps — completing the back-office, the maintenance module, or a deploy/CI pass?

Ticketing's done. Now the landlord app — you're already `cd`'d into `mobile-landlord`. Install and start it in web mode:

```powershell
npm install
npm start
```

(The `start` script uses `expo start --offline` to dodge the `api.expo.dev` fetch error we hit before.) When it's up, press `w` in that terminal to open the web build, or go to the URL it prints. Log in with `owner@demo.test`, grab the OTP from the API console, and you should land on the **Dashboard** tab (active leases, collected this period, collection rate, arrears + portfolio list) with an **Approvals** tab for the application funnel (Screen → Approve → Reject).

Two things to watch for, both from earlier apps:

If `npm install` chokes on peer-dep conflicts, re-run as `npm install --legacy-peer-deps`.

Make sure the API is still running on `:3000` and CORS is enabled (it is — `app.enableCors()` is in `main.ts`), otherwise the browser console shows a CORS error and the dashboard stays empty.

Fire it up and paste any error or a screenshot — if it comes up clean, that's all three frontends plus the full backend verified, and I'll give you the whole-system status rundown.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-03 10:14

One thing worth a glance: the dashboard shows **Collection rate 100%** while **Arrears R9 200** and Unit 101 reads "R9 200 due." Those aren't contradictory — collection rate is measured within the selected period (2026-08: R9 200 invoiced, R9 200 collected = 100%), while arrears is the cumulative outstanding balance carried across periods. But if you'd rather the two read consistently (e.g. rate net of prior arrears), that's a one-line change in the metric calc — say the word.

Where the system stands now, end to end and verified live:

The **backend** is a NestJS modular monolith on Postgres with forced row-level security per vendor, covering auth (passwordless OTP → JWT), properties/leasing, a double-entry billing engine with recurring invoicing and dunning, payments via the Stitch/Paystack provider layer with idempotent webhooks, owners with trust-account deposits and split payouts, expenses, notifications, documents + e-sign, a public listings/applications funnel that auto-provisions a lease on approval, and now maintenance/ticketing that posts contractor costs to the ledger. Sixteen pure-logic test suites are green.

The **frontends** are all standing up against it: the tenant app (login → view rent → pay → webhook settle), the Next.js web back-office (rent roll, collections, owners, applications), and the landlord app you just ran (dashboard + approvals).

The main thing still outstanding from earlier is deployment — getting this onto your Hetzner box with managed Postgres and a CI pipeline that runs tests/build on push, plus committing everything to git. Want to tackle that next, or is there another module or polish item you'd rather do first?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-03 11:05

Good news: the branding all works — logo tile, themed footer with contact details, accent metric. The problem you spotted is a real data-logic bug, and it's the same root issue from before resurfacing.

Look at the aging row: every bucket (0–30, 31–60, 61–90, 90+) is R0, yet Total is R9 200. That's because the buckets measure `today − due_date`, and that R9 200 invoice **isn't overdue yet** — its due date is still in the future. So it's *outstanding* but not *in arrears*, and it falls into none of the past-due buckets while still counting toward the total. The table has no column for "owed but not yet due," so it looks broken.

The fix: add a "Not yet due" column so the row reconciles (Not yet due + overdue buckets = Total), and label things honestly. Let me look at the reporting query.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-03 12:53

Fixed. The aging table was measuring "days past due" but that R9 200 invoice isn't overdue yet — its due date is still in the future — so it counted toward the total while landing in none of the past-due buckets. That's why every bucket read R0 but Total showed R9 200.

What I changed:

The backend `arrearsAging` now returns a `notYetDue` bucket plus a true `arrears` figure (overdue only), and the columns reconcile exactly: `Not yet due + 0–30 + 31–60 + 61–90 + 90+ = Total`. The web table now shows those columns with a one-line explanation, so R9 200 sits under "Not yet due," arrears reads R0, and the total makes sense. I also renamed the top metric from the misleading "Arrears (total)" to "Outstanding," and made the mobile card match (labelled "Outstanding," red only when there's genuinely overdue money).

Separately, that `JSON.parse: unexpected end of data` banner was the fetch helper choking when an endpoint returns an empty 200 body — I made `req()` in all three apps tolerant of empty responses, so it returns null instead of crashing the load.

To see it: restart the API (picks up the reporting change) and refresh the web console — no migration needed for this fix. Since you'd set the landlord app's slug to `rivonia`, reloading it will also show the navy/Poppins Rivonia theme, confirming the brand swap.

Two housekeeping notes: `tsconfig.tmpcheck.json` in the project root couldn't be removed from here — safe to delete manually. And the mount kept truncating editor-tool writes this session, so I rewrote the affected files via shell; everything now typechecks clean across backend, web, and both mobile apps.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-04 09:43

All three feature UIs are built and everything typechecks clean across the backend and all three apps. Here's what's new:

**Tenant app** — a Maintenance screen (reached via the new "Report" action on the dashboard). Tenants pick a category and priority, describe the issue, and it files against their active lease's unit. Below the form is their request history, and when a request is marked resolved they get an "Approve & close" button.

**Landlord app** — a new Maintenance tab. Every ticket shows its priority/status, and the action adapts to state: Assign work order → Start work → Complete (with a cost field that posts the expense to the ledger). Resolved tickets show "awaiting tenant approval."

**Web back-office** — the Owners page now has per-owner statement history. Click "View statements" on an owner to see all their statements (gross, fee, expenses, net, status), generate one for a period, and pay out any finalized statement right from the row.

Backend-wise this only needed two new read endpoints (`GET /maintenance/work-orders`, `GET /owners/:id/statements`) — no migration, so nothing schema-level to run.

To try it live: restart the API (picks up the two new routes), then reload the apps. Full loop to test — tenant files a request → landlord assigns/starts/completes with a cost → tenant approves & closes; and on web, generate an owner statement then pay it out.

One reminder from before: the landlord app's slug is still `rivonia`, which has no seeded tickets/leases, so its Maintenance tab will look empty. Point it back to `demo` (in `mobile-landlord/src/config.ts`) to exercise the flow against the seeded demo data where the tenant (`thabo@demo.test`) and demo units live.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-04 10:33

A PowerShell smoke-test suite in `scripts/api-tests/` that drives the exact endpoints each app screen calls, so you can verify the flows without clicking through the UI.

How it works: login is passwordless OTP, so `login.ps1` requests a code (printed to your API console), you paste it, and the JWT is cached under `.tokens/` and reused by the other scripts until it expires.

```powershell
cd C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3\scripts\api-tests
./test-branding.ps1     # public /branding/demo + /rivonia, then owner self-service edit
./test-tenant.ps1       # profile, invoices, lease, file a ticket, pay rent   (thabo@demo.test)
./test-landlord.ps1     # dashboard, assign→start→complete a ticket, owner statement (owner@demo.test)
./test-all.ps1          # everything in sequence
```

Each step prints `[PASS]`/`[FAIL]` with the JSON, so you see exactly what the app would receive. `test-branding.ps1`'s public part needs no login at all — good first thing to run to confirm the API is up. Run `test-tenant.ps1` before `test-landlord.ps1` so there's a fresh open ticket for the landlord script to work through.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-06 12:03

Here's the full runbook for the whole system on your Windows/PowerShell setup. Do the backend first (everything depends on it), then whichever frontend you want.

## 1. Backend + database (the API everything talks to)

```powershell
cd C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3

npm install                     # first time only
docker compose up -d            # Postgres on :5433, Redis on :6380
Copy-Item .env.example .env     # first time only (skip if you already have .env)
```

One-time database setup (creates the least-privileged app role, schema, and demo data):

```powershell
# create the pms_app role (once)
Get-Content scripts/setup-app-role.sql | docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U pms -d pms

npm run migration:run           # creates tables + RLS policies (re-run after new migrations)
npm run seed                    # demo vendor, owner, unit, tenant
```

Start the API (leave this window running):

```powershell
npm run start:dev               # http://localhost:3000/api
```

## 2. Web back-office (Next.js console)

```powershell
cd C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3\web-admin
npm install                     # first time (pulls Tailwind + lucide)
npm run dev                     # http://localhost:3001
```

## 3. Mobile apps (Expo — tenant & landlord)

```powershell
cd C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3\mobile-tenant
npm install
npx expo install expo-blur expo-linear-gradient @expo-google-fonts/plus-jakarta-sans   # first time
npm start                       # then press w for web, or scan the QR in Expo Go
```

Same for the landlord app (`cd ..\mobile-landlord`, same three commands).

## Logging in

Auth is passwordless — the OTP prints to the **API window** (step 1), not sent anywhere.

- Web console & landlord app: `owner@demo.test`
- Tenant app: `thabo@demo.test`

Request a code in the app, read the 6 digits from the API console, enter them.

## Quick reference

Ports: API `3000`, web `3001`, Postgres `5433`, Redis `6380`, Expo `8081`. The `demo` vendor has the seeded data; `rivonia` (`owner@rivonia.test`) exists for brand-swapping only.

Day-to-day after the first setup, it's just three windows: `npm run start:dev` (API), `npm run dev` (web), `npm start` (each mobile app). Only re-run `migration:run` when there are new migrations, and only re-run the installs when I've added a package. If you'd like, I can drop this into a `RUN.md` in the project so it's always at hand.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-07 13:22

based on the roadmap what features are still outstanding or can be added?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-07 13:23

Here's where things stand against the roadmap in `README.md`, and what's genuinely left to build.

**Phase 0–1 (foundations + "collect rent")** — essentially complete. Multi-tenancy/RLS, OTP+JWT auth, white-label branding, properties/units/leases, VAT invoicing, double-entry ledger, recurring billing, Stitch payments, dunning, and the tenant + landlord mobile apps are all working end-to-end. The one soft gap is **observability** (structured logging, metrics, error tracking) — scaffolded intent, not really built.

**Phase 2 (operations & agencies)** — mostly there on the backend, with **missing UIs**. These modules exist server-side but have little or no front-end:

- **Documents & e-sign** — full backend (presigned storage, signature requests, webhooks) but no screen anywhere to upload a lease, send it for signature, or download docs. Biggest UI gap.
- **Inspections** — `InspectionsModule` is registered but has no app surface (move-in/move-out inspections, condition reports, photos).
- **In-app messaging** — `CommsModule` exists; there's no chat/thread UI between tenant, agency, and owner. Notifications currently only log to console — real channels (SMS/email/push providers) aren't wired.
- **Owner portal** — owners get statements/payouts computed, but there's no owner-facing login/app to see their own properties and payouts.

**Phase 3 (growth)** — partially done. Listings→application→approval funnel works. Still open:

- **Reporting depth** — you have rent roll, arrears aging, and collection rate; missing are income/expense statements, a proper ledger/trial-balance view, VAT reports, and CSV/PDF exports.
- **Localization / full config** — single language/currency today; no i18n or per-market config beyond the ZA policy pack.
- **Trust-account formalization** — deposit trust accounting exists but isn't reconciled against real bank data.

**Phase 4 (scale)** — barely started. `ApiKeysModule` + an external API/webhooks controller exist (API-key auth, HMAC), but there's no developer portal, no AI maintenance triage, and no IoT/smart-meter integration.

**Cross-cutting things worth adding regardless of phase:** automated test coverage (only pure-logic unit suites today — no e2e), a CI pipeline, deployment to your Hetzner box, real payment/e-sign providers (swap the stubs), and lease escalations/renewals (the `escalation` field exists but nothing acts on it).

If I had to rank the highest-value next builds: **(1)** documents + e-sign UI, **(2)** the owner portal, **(3)** reporting exports, **(4)** real notification channels, then **(5)** deploy + CI to make it live. Want me to pick one and build it — or want a short written plan for any of them?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-07 15:09

Done — the payout is now tied to the owner's bank account.

Backend: `payout()` refuses to run if the owner has no captured banking (`accountNumber`), returning "Add this owner's banking details before paying out," and it passes the owner's account (bank, holder, account number, branch code, type) through to the payment provider's `PayoutRequest.bankAccount`, logging the masked destination. So a payout always goes to that specific owner's account.

Web (Owners → statements panel): the header now shows where money will go — "Payouts to FNB ••5678" — or, if the owner has no banking, a red "No banking details — add them to enable payouts" link that opens the banking editor. The **Pay out** button on each statement is enabled only when banking is present; otherwise it shows "Add banking first." Saving banking immediately unlocks the button (no reload needed).

No migration this turn (the `owners.banking` column came with the previous change) — just restart the API and refresh the web console. If you haven't yet run the previous step's `npm run migration:run` + `npm run seed`, do that first so the banking column exists and the demo owners have accounts.

So the flow is now end-to-end: capture the owner's banking on the Owners page → generate their statement → Pay out sends the net amount to that account (and it's blocked until the account exists). `tsconfig.tmpcheck.json` in the root is still safe to delete.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-07 18:01

what's features are missing or what can be improved -  besides the deployment CI/CD

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-07 18:02

Good question — plenty of runway beyond deploy/CI. Grouping by type, with the highest-impact things called out.

**Functional gaps (features that aren't there yet)**

- **In-app messaging** — the `comms` module is still a health-only stub; there's no tenant ↔ agency ↔ owner thread anywhere. This is the last big Phase‑2 feature.
- **Owner portal** — owners have records, statements, banking, and payouts, but no login/app of their own to see their properties, income, and payout history.
- **Property & unit management UI** — you can't create or edit properties/units from the web; they only appear via the seed or an approved application. That's a surprising hole for day-to-day use.
- **Real providers** — payments (Stitch/Paystack), e-sign, and all notification channels (SMS/email/push) are dev stubs. Notifications only log to console.
- **Landlord mobile parity** — listings, applications, owner statements, reports, and the new pages are web-only; the landlord app can't do them.
- **Link work orders to service providers** — you now have a provider directory, but a work order's `contractorId` isn't wired to it (assign a provider, auto-notify them, track their jobs).
- **Payments depth** — card payments, recurring debit-order mandates (DebiCheck), payment plans for arrears, PDF receipts/tax invoices, and refunds.
- **Localization / multi-currency** — single language and ZAR only.

**Engineering quality / hardening**

- **Security** — banking details and account numbers are stored as plaintext JSONB; those should be encrypted at rest or tokenized (and matters for POPIA). Also: per-route rate limiting, consistent DTO validation (class-validator), an audit log, and the unused membership `scope`/RBAC granularity.
- **Testing** — only pure-logic unit suites exist; no integration/e2e/API-contract or frontend tests.
- **Observability** — no structured logging, request tracing, metrics, or error tracking (e.g. Sentry); add readiness/liveness probes.
- **Pagination** — list endpoints (tickets, owners, notifications, documents, providers) return everything; they'll need pagination + server-side filtering/sorting at scale.
- **Job resilience** — dead-letter handling, retry/backoff tuning, and a queue-monitoring view for BullMQ.

**UX / product polish**

- Replace the browser `prompt()`/`confirm()` dialogs (Applications screen, API-key revoke, e-sign) with proper modals, and add a toast system instead of inline error strips.
- Dashboard **trend charts** over time, plus global search and table sorting/pagination.
- A **new-vendor onboarding wizard** and a **staff-invite / roles** UI (assign property managers).
- Mobile: real push notifications and offline handling.

**Compliance (ZA-specific, since that's the launch market)**

- **POPIA**: consent tracking and data export/erasure, plus the PII encryption above.
- **PPRA/trust**: surface FFC/trust-account status in the UI and add trust-reconciliation reports.
- **VAT**: proper tax invoices with the VAT number and credit notes.

If I had to pick the **top 5 next builds** by value-to-effort: (1) property/unit management UI — it's a core gap and quick; (2) wire work orders to service providers; (3) encrypt banking/PII; (4) in-app messaging; (5) the owner portal. Want me to start on any of these — property/unit CRUD is the fastest win and unblocks a lot?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 19:19

In-app messaging is built end-to-end across all four surfaces.

**Backend** — a `comms` module with `conversations` + `messages` tables (vendor-scoped, forced RLS, migration `1720000016000`). Threads are between one tenant and the vendor's staff, with per-side read watermarks so each side gets accurate unread counts. Routes under `/messages`: `mine` (tenant's threads), `inbox` (staff, all threads), `conversations/:id` (thread view — marks the viewer's side read), `conversations` (start), `:id/reply`, `:id/status` (close/reopen), and `unread-count`. Role is inferred from the JWT, so the same reply endpoint serves both sides and a reply to a closed thread reopens it.

**Web console** — a new Messages page (in the sidebar) with a master–detail inbox: tenant list on the left with unread dots, a chat thread on the right with left/right bubbles, an Enter-to-send composer, and a Close/Reopen toggle.

**Landlord app** — a Messages tab in the frosted pill nav (chat icon). Staff inbox with avatars and unread dots, tap into a thread, reply, and close/reopen.

**Tenant app** — a Messages screen reached from a new Home quick-action tile. Tenants see their threads, tap "New" to start a conversation with the property manager (subject + message), and reply in a familiar chat view.

The seed now creates three demo threads on `demo` (Thabo's geyser leak with a staff reply, Kagiso's parking query awaiting staff, and Lerato's closed lease-renewal chat). Typechecks are clean on the backend, web, and both apps.

To see it live, run `npm run migration:run`, `npm run seed`, and restart the API. Two housekeeping files sit in the project root that the sandbox can't delete — `tsconfig.tmpcheck.json` and now `tsconfig.seedcheck.json`; both are safe to remove.

That clears the messaging item. Remaining from the shortlist: encrypt banking/PII (POPIA) or the owner portal. Want the next one?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 19:27

The owner portal is built — a role-scoped area of the web console for property owners (investors), not the agency staff.

**Backend** — added an `owner` role and linked owner records to a login user (`owners.user_id`, migration `1720000017000`). A new `/portal` API (owner-role only) returns strictly that owner's own data, resolved from their user id and filtered by `owner_id`: `summary` (properties, occupancy, monthly rent, paid-to-date, awaiting-payout, latest statement), `properties` (per-property unit/occupancy/rent rollups), `statements` (each joined to its payout), and `banking` (get/update).

**Web** — signing in as an owner now redirects to `/portal` instead of the back-office (role read from the JWT). The shell renders distinct portal chrome — a slim nav of Overview, Statements, Properties, Banking — while staff still get the full sidebar. Four glass pages:
- **Overview**: metric cards, an occupancy bar, latest-statement summary, and a prompt to add banking if missing.
- **Statements**: period-by-period collected / fee / net payout with paid-out vs awaiting-payout status.
- **Properties**: cards with occupancy and monthly rent per property.
- **Banking**: the owner edits their own payout account (feeds the same provider-gated payout flow).

**Seed** — `sipho@owner.demo.test` is now an owner login for Sipho Dlamini (two managed properties, a paid-out statement, a current awaiting-payout statement, and banking on file). Backend, web, and the seed all typecheck clean; RUN.md documents the new login.

To try it: run `npm run migration:run`, `npm run seed`, restart the API, then log into the web console as `sipho@owner.demo.test`. A couple of temp `tsconfig.*check*.json` files remain in the root that the sandbox can't delete — all safe to remove.

That covers the owner portal. The last item on the shortlist is encrypting banking/PII for POPIA. Want me to take it?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 20:12

That error means another process is already holding port 3000 — almost certainly a previous `start:dev` that didn't fully exit (the `^C` may have left the ts-node child alive). Your new instance can't bind, so kill the old one first.

In PowerShell:

```powershell
# See what's on 3000
netstat -ano | findstr :3000

# Kill it by PID (last column from the line above), e.g.:
Stop-Process -Id <PID> -Force
```

Or do it in one line:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 | Select-Object -Expand OwningProcess -Unique | ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_ -Force }
```

Then start again:

```powershell
npm run start:dev
```

If it keeps happening, it's usually because Ctrl+C left the `ts-node-dev`/`nest start --watch` child process running while the parent died. A blunt fix is to clear any stray Node processes before starting:

```powershell
Get-Process node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
```

(That kills *all* Node processes, so don't run it if you have the web-admin or Expo dev servers you want to keep — those are on 3001/8081, separate windows.)

Want me to add a short "port already in use" entry to the RUN.md troubleshooting section?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 20:17

Same thing on 3001 — a previous `next dev` is still holding the web port. Free it:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3001 | Select-Object -Expand OwningProcess -Unique | ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_ -Force }
```

Then:

```powershell
npm run dev
```

If you'd rather not hunt the PID, you can just point this run at a different port:

```powershell
next dev -p 3002
```

(but then open the site at `http://localhost:3002`).

These stale-port situations keep coming up, so it's worth a runbook entry. Want me to add a "Port already in use (EADDRINUSE)" section to RUN.md covering both 3000 and 3001?

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-08 20:18

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 20:18

Run this in PowerShell from the project root — it frees port 3000, then starts the API on it:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen |
  Select-Object -Expand OwningProcess -Unique |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_ -Force }

npm run start:dev
```

The first command finds whatever is listening on 3000 and force-kills it; the second starts your API and takes the port.

If `Get-NetTCPConnection` isn't available on your setup, the netstat equivalent works too:

```powershell
$pid = (netstat -ano | Select-String ':3000\s.*LISTENING' | ForEach-Object { ($_ -split '\s+')[-1] } | Select-Object -First 1)
if ($pid) { Stop-Process -Id $pid -Force }
npm run start:dev
```

Either way, if the killed process was a stray `nest start --watch`/ts-node from a Ctrl+C that didn't clean up, this is exactly the right fix — it's your own old server, safe to kill. Want me to drop this into RUN.md as a troubleshooting entry so it's handy next time?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 20:23

Done. `scripts/start-all.ps1` starts the whole stack. From the project root:

```powershell
.\scripts\start-all.ps1
```

What it does, in order: brings up Docker (Postgres/Redis), frees ports 3000/3001/8081/8082 so nothing blocks the launch (that's the EADDRINUSE fix baked in), then opens each app in its own titled PowerShell window — API on 3000, web on 3001, and the two Expo apps on 8081/8082. It prints the URLs and demo logins at the end.

Flags:
- `-Setup` — first run or after pulling new migrations: `npm install` everywhere, `migration:run`, and `seed` before starting.
- `-NoMobile` — just the API + web back-office.
- `-NoKill` — leave the ports alone (don't stop what's already there).

One gotcha: if PowerShell refuses to run it ("running scripts is disabled"), allow it once with `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`. I also added this to RUN.md's day-to-day section.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 20:32

Notice the API actually booted fully (every route mapped, "Nest application successfully started") — it only failed on the very last step, binding 3000. That means a *different, older* server is still holding the port. Your earlier kill either missed it or it respawned.

The likely culprit: an old `npm run start:dev` window is still open somewhere. `ts-node-dev` runs with `--respawn`, so if that window is alive it keeps a Node process on 3000 and re-launches it when killed. So:

1. First, look for and **close any other PowerShell window** still running the API.
2. Then force-free the port and confirm nothing comes back:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen |
  Select-Object -Expand OwningProcess -Unique |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_ -Force }

# confirm it's clear
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

If that second command prints nothing, the port is free — start the API again.

If it *keeps* coming back after you kill it, the respawning parent is still alive. Clear all Node processes (only do this if you don't have other Node servers you want to keep — the web/Expo ones can be restarted):

```powershell
Get-Process node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
npm run start:dev
```

Want me to add a `-KillOnly` switch to `start-all.ps1` (frees the ports and exits, no launching) so you have a one-command "clear everything" — plus fold this into the RUN.md troubleshooting section?

Worth knowing for later: that per-app `VENDOR_SLUG` in `src/config.ts` is exactly how the white-label swap is demoed — set both apps to the same slug for a consistent look, or point one at `rivonia` to show a different tenant's branding.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-08 21:26

what's missing?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-08 21:26

Here's the honest gap list for PMS0.3, grouped by priority. Everything functional is built — what's missing is mostly production-hardening and a few polish items.

**Security / compliance (highest priority)**
- **Banking & PII encryption (POPIA)** — owner/tenant banking details and contact info are stored as plain JSON. This was the last shortlist item and is the most important thing still outstanding for a SA product handling money.
- No audit trail on sensitive reads/writes (who viewed/changed banking, payouts, etc.).

**Production readiness**
- **Real providers** — payment (Stitch/Paystack), notifications (email/SMS/push), and e-sign are all dev stubs. Needs live integrations + webhook signature verification.
- **Deployment / CI-CD** — explicitly deferred; no pipeline, containerised deploy, env/secrets management, or migrations-on-deploy.
- **Automated tests + observability** — no unit/integration/e2e suite, no logging/metrics/error tracking (Sentry etc.), no health/readiness probes.
- **Rate limiting is present (throttler) but not tuned; no backups/DR story.**

**Feature gaps**
- **Real-time messaging** — the inbox works but relies on manual refresh; no WebSocket/push so new messages don't arrive live, and there's no push notification when a tenant/staff replies.
- **Table pagination / search** — lists (properties, applications, notifications, statements) load everything; fine for demo, not at scale.
- **Localization / i18n** — English + ZAR only.
- Owner portal is read-mostly (statements/properties/banking); no owner-facing documents or messaging.

**Nice-to-have polish**
- The two temp `tsconfig.*check*.json` files still sit in the repo root (sandbox couldn't delete them).
- A few flows could still move off inline editing into the new modals for consistency.

If I had to pick the single most valuable next step, it's **encrypting banking/PII** — it's the one genuine risk item, it's backend-only, and it closes out the original shortlist. Want me to take that on?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-09 07:56

Owner banking is now encrypted at rest. Summary:

**Encryption (`src/common/security/pii-crypto.ts`)** — AES-256-GCM (authenticated) with a key derived via scrypt from `PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Values are stored as a self-describing envelope (`{__enc, iv, tag, ct}`) inside the existing `jsonb` column, so there's **no column-type migration** and legacy plaintext rows stay readable (they re-encrypt next time they're saved). Decryption failures fail closed with a clear error.

**Transparent wiring** — a TypeORM value transformer on `Owner.banking` encrypts on write and decrypts on read, so every existing path (owner statements/payout, portal, owners service) keeps working with a plain object and never touches ciphertext.

**Data minimisation (POPIA)** — the staff owners *list* now returns **masked** account numbers (`••••1234` + last-4 only). Full details are returned solely by a new manager-gated `GET /owners/:id/banking`, which the web banking editor fetches on demand when you click "Banking". The owner's own portal still sees their full details. Payout logs were already masked.

**Config & demo** — added `PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to `.env.example` (documented: keep stable and secret in prod; blank = insecure dev key). The seed now writes Sipho's and Acme's banking as real encrypted envelopes, so the demo DB is genuinely encrypted, not plaintext.

Backend, web, and the seed all typecheck clean. To activate: set `PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in `.env`, restart the API, and `npm run seed` to lay down encrypted demo data.

One scoping note I'd flag: I deliberately left user **email/phone** unencrypted because they're used as login/OTP lookup keys — encrypting them would break `WHERE email = …` auth queries. Doing those properly needs deterministic/blind-index encryption, which is a larger, separate piece. Banking was the real exposure and it's now closed.

That clears the last item on the shortlist. What's left is all production-hardening (real payment/notification/e-sign providers, CI/CD, tests + observability, real-time messaging). Want to tackle any of those, or is this a good stopping point?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-12 17:37

All done — the full production-hardening pass landed, finishing with CI/CD. Everything typechecks and all **67 tests pass**.

**Real providers** (every one degrades to a safe stub when credentials are absent, so dev/CI need no secrets):
- **Payments** — real Paystack over `fetch` (transaction initialize + transfer-recipient/transfer for payouts), env-gated.
- **Notifications** — real SendGrid email + Twilio SMS; the module picks the real gateway per channel when creds exist, else console.
- **E-sign** — generic HTTP provider (`ESIGN_API_URL`), falls back to the native link.

**Observability** — `/api/health` (liveness) and `/api/health/ready` (Postgres + Redis checks, 503 when down), a request-logging interceptor with an `x-request-id` correlation id, and a global exception filter with a consistent error envelope. Graceful shutdown hooks enabled.

**Real-time messaging** — an in-process event bus + an SSE endpoint `GET /api/messages/stream?token=…` (JWT verified from the query since EventSource can't set headers; staff get vendor-wide events, tenants only their own). The web console now updates the inbox and open thread live.

**Tests** — added specs for the PII crypto round-trip/tamper-detection/masking, the Paystack stub fallback, and the SSE event bus. Suite grew from 57 → 67.

**CI/CD (the finisher)** —
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: tests + build for API and web on every PR/push.
- `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`: on a `v*` tag, builds and pushes API + web images to GHCR (built-in token), with a `production` environment deploy hook.
- `Dockerfile` (API, with health check) + `web-admin/Dockerfile` (Next standalone) + `.dockerignore`s + `compose.prod.yml`.
- `DEPLOY.md` documents it all; new env vars added to `.env.example`; RUN.md points to DEPLOY.md.

One real fix surfaced along the way: `tsconfig.build.json` had no `include`, so `nest build` was pulling in the mobile apps' `.tsx` — I scoped it to `src/`, and confirmed a clean compile emits `dist/main.js`.

Leftovers the sandbox couldn't delete (safe to remove): `tsconfig.tmpcheck.json`, `tsconfig.seedcheck.json`, `tsconfig.seedchk2.json`, `tsconfig.ci.json`.

That closes out the entire hardening list. The codebase is now demo-complete with production-grade providers, health/observability, live messaging, a green test suite, and a working CI/CD pipeline.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-16 12:40

Peach Payments, Yoco, and PayFast are integrated as first-class collection gateways. All 74 tests pass and the backend typechecks clean.

**New providers** (each implements the existing `PaymentProvider` interface, so billing/accounting code is untouched, and each degrades to a safe local stub when its credentials are absent):
- **PayFast** — redirect flow. `collect` builds the signed `…/eng/process` redirect URL (md5 signature over the URL-encoded params + optional passphrase, sandbox/live switch via `PAYFAST_SANDBOX`). No server call needed to start.
- **Yoco** — Checkout API. One `fetch` to `payments.yoco.com/api/checkouts` returns the hosted redirect URL.
- **Peach Payments** — hosted checkout via a configurable endpoint + bearer token (`PEACH_CHECKOUT_URL`/`PEACH_BEARER_TOKEN`, since Peach's OAuth/entity setup is environment-specific), returning the redirect URL.

**Collection ↔ payout split** — these consumer gateways can't do arbitrary owner bank payouts, so I decoupled the rails:
- `PAYMENT_PROVIDER` selects the **collection** rail: `stitch | paystack | payfast | yoco | peach`.
- `PAYOUT_PROVIDER` selects the **owner-payout** rail: `paystack | stitch` (default paystack).

So a vendor can collect rent through PayFast/Yoco/Peach while owner statements still pay out through a payout-capable rail. Owner-statement payouts now inject `PAYOUT_PROVIDER`, and the three new providers' `payout()` throws a clear "not supported — set PAYOUT_PROVIDER to a payout-capable rail" error.

**Webhooks** — added `/api/payments/webhook/{payfast,yoco,peach}`. Yoco/Peach use the existing HMAC guard (`YOCO_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET`); PayFast's ITN is verified with its md5 signature against `PAYFAST_PASSPHRASE`, mapping `payment_status=COMPLETE` and the `pf_<invoiceId>` reference back through the idempotent `confirm()` path. Peach success is matched on `000.000/000.100` result codes.

**Config, tests, docs** — added all gateway env vars to `.env.example`, 7 new tests (PayFast signature determinism + passphrase sensitivity + signed-URL build, Yoco/Peach stub fallback, payout refusal), and updated `DEPLOY.md`'s env table with the two-rail model.

One production note: the collection gateways are redirect-based, so the tenant apps should open `redirectUrl` from the initiate response in a browser/WebView, and you'll want to confirm the exact webhook payload shape against each provider's current docs (I mapped the common fields and success codes, but versions drift). The signing and money-in/confirmation plumbing is all in place.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-18 07:02

I ran a real audit rather than a rubber stamp, and it found genuine problems. **78 tests pass, all four codebases typecheck.** Here's the honest picture.

## Critical issues found and fixed

**1. OTP brute-force — the serious one.** `attempts` was incremented on every wrong guess but *never checked*. A 6-digit code could be walked through by repeated requests. Fixed with a real lockout (`OTP_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, default 5) that burns the challenge — and I added a 4-case regression test proving even the *correct* code is refused after the limit.

**2. Insecure defaults would boot silently in production.** `JWT_SECRET` fell back to `'change-me-in-prod'` and the PII key to a dev constant. Added `validateEnv()` which **refuses to start** in production if JWT/PII keys, `DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`, or `CORS_ORIGINS` are missing/default, or if `OTP_CHANNEL=console` (which prints one-time codes into your logs). In dev these are warnings.

**3. CORS reflected any origin with credentials.** Now an explicit allowlist from `CORS_ORIGINS`; production denies by default rather than reflecting.

**4. No security headers.** Added a dependency-free middleware (nosniff, DENY framing, HSTS in prod, referrer/permissions policy) and disabled `x-powered-by`.

**5. Auth endpoints shared the global 120/min limit.** OTP request is now 5/min and verify 10/min — brute-force targets shouldn't sit on the default bucket.

**6. Mobile apps hardcoded `http://localhost:3000`** — a hard blocker for any real build. Both now read `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE`.

## Verified healthy
`synchronize: false` (schema only via migrations), RLS forced per-vendor, banking encrypted at rest with masked staff listings, webhook HMAC verification, double-entry ledger, health/readiness probes, graceful shutdown, CI/CD green.

## Remaining risks — my honest read

**Not production-ready without these:**
- **`npm audit`: 14 vulns (3 high)** — `lodash` code injection, `multer` DoS, and a `uuid` bounds issue. The fixes need breaking upgrades (`@nestjs/typeorm@11`). This needs a deliberate upgrade pass with the suite as your safety net; I didn't force it because it would likely break the build mid-audit.
- **No load/failure testing.** The SSE bus is in-process, so it only works single-instance — multi-instance deploys need Redis pub/sub behind that same interface.
- **Payment gateway payloads are unverified against live sandboxes.** I mapped documented fields, but you must run a sandbox transaction per gateway before taking real money.
- **No backup/restore or DR drill**, and no error tracking (Sentry) wired.
- **Email/phone remain unencrypted** (they're auth lookup keys — needs blind-index encryption).

Fair summary: it's now **secure enough for a pilot with real users**, but I would not call it production-ready until the dependency upgrade and a live sandbox payment test are done. Want me to take the dependency upgrade next?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-18 07:25

I have to be straight with you: **I could not complete the upgrade**, and the reason is environmental, not a code problem.

**What blocked it:** this sandbox terminates background processes between tool calls, so every `npm install` got ~45 seconds before being killed. A NestJS 10→11 upgrade pulls ~1000 packages. I tried three ways — direct install, background install with polling, and a scratch copy on fast local disk — and all were killed mid-flight. I also briefly misread `pgrep` output as "still running" when the process had already died; I corrected that once I checked properly.

**Your repo is verified untouched:** `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are byte-identical to the backup I took, `@nestjs/core` is still 10.4.22, there's no partial-install residue, and all **78 tests pass**. Nothing is half-upgraded.

**The genuinely useful finding** — I did the reachability analysis, and the scary numbers are mostly theoretical here:

- **multer DoS (high) — not reachable.** No `FileInterceptor`/`UploadedFile`/multipart anywhere; documents use pre-signed storage URLs. Multer is never invoked.
- **lodash `_.template` injection (high) — not reachable.** Not a direct dependency; used internally by `@nestjs/config` for lookups, never with user input.
- **qs/express DoS (moderate) — low.** Targets `qs.stringify`; the server parses, behind rate limits.
- **uuid (moderate) — not reachable.** Only the `buf` form of v3/v5/v6; TypeORM uses v4.

So this is a **hygiene upgrade, not an active incident** — which matters, because it means you can schedule it rather than rush it.

**What I delivered instead:**
- **`UPGRADE.md`** — the exact one-shot command (the whole `@nestjs/*` family must move together or npm hits the peer conflict I ran into), the reachability table above, the Express 5 breaking changes to watch, verification steps, and a rollback.
- **CI supply-chain gate** — `ci.yml` now runs `npm audit` on every push: blocking on critical, plus a visible non-blocking report. So when you run the upgrade natively (~2 min in PowerShell), **CI validates it for you automatically** — that's a better verification than my sandbox could have given anyway.

Bottom line: the security fixes from the audit are done and tested; the dependency refresh is a documented, low-risk task that needs to run on your machine. Run the command in `UPGRADE.md` on a branch and push — if CI goes green, you're clear.

Everything for the Contabo move is ready. Two parts:

**1. A production-critical fix — OTP delivery.** This wasn't optional: your prod env-guard (correctly) refuses to boot with `OTP_CHANNEL=console`, and delivery was still stubbed — so **nobody could log in on the VPS**. I wired `AuthService.deliver()` to send the code through the real notification channel (SendGrid email for email logins, Twilio SMS for phone), with a safe console fallback, and added an env-guard that stops boot if you pick `email`/`sms` without the matching provider key. Injected optionally so existing tests are unaffected; backend typechecks clean.

**2. Deploy assets + runbook**, tailored to `vmi3453343` / `169.58.46.223`:
- `docs/CONTABO-DEPLOY.md` — the full step-by-step: DNS records, hardening, code, secrets, `up -d`, DB init, OTP setup, payments, backups, day-to-day, troubleshooting.
- `deploy/harden.sh` — one-shot server hardening: non-root `deploy` user + your SSH key, UFW (22/80/443 only), fail2ban, unattended upgrades, key-only SSH, Docker install.
- `deploy/compose.prod.yml` — Caddy (auto-HTTPS) in front of web + api, with Postgres & Redis; only Caddy exposes ports.
- `deploy/Caddyfile` — auto Let's Encrypt for `app.` and `api.` your domain.
- `deploy/.env.prod.example` — every required secret with generation commands; `.gitignore` updated so `.env.prod` and backups never get committed.
- `deploy/backup.sh` — nightly `pg_dump`, 14-day retention.

**The short path on the box:**
```bash
# DNS: app.example.com + api.example.com  ->  169.58.46.223
ssh root@169.58.46.223 && bash harden.sh "ssh-ed25519 AAAA...you"
ssh deploy@169.58.46.223
git clone <repo> pms && cd pms
cp deploy/.env.prod.example deploy/.env.prod   # fill in (openssl rand -hex 32 ×2)
# edit deploy/Caddyfile with your domain
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec api npm run migration:run
```

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-20 11:57

Done. Tagged releases now auto-deploy to your Contabo VPS.

**How it works** (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, valid YAML):
1. **`images` job** — builds the API and web images and pushes them to GHCR, tagged with the semver + `latest`. The web image is built with `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE` baked in from a repo variable, so the client points at your real API domain.
2. **`deploy` job** — SSHes into the VPS (`appleboy/ssh-action`), checks out the tag, logs in to GHCR, and rolls out with the new **`deploy/compose.prod.images.yml`** (which *pulls* the images rather than rebuilding on the 2-core box), runs `migration:run`, then hits `/api/health/ready` to confirm it's up and prunes old images.

It runs on `git push` of a `v*` tag (or manual dispatch), and is gated on the GitHub **production** environment so you can require an approval before it ships.

**One-time setup** (documented in `docs/CONTABO-DEPLOY.md §10`): clone the repo on the box as `deploy` with `deploy/.env.prod` filled, add a CI deploy SSH key, and set these repo secrets — `VPS_HOST` (169.58.46.223), `VPS_USER` (deploy), `VPS_SSH_KEY`, `VPS_APP_DIR` (/home/deploy/pms), `GHCR_USER`, `GHCR_TOKEN` (read:packages) — plus the variable `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE`.

**Then every release is just:**
```bash
git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0
```

Design choice worth noting: I went registry-based (build in CI, pull on the box) rather than build-on-server — faster deploys and no memory pressure on the VPS during a release, and it reuses the image pipeline you already had. The build-on-server `compose.prod.yml` is still there for the first manual bootstrap.

Same two caveats as before still stand: the Jest suite couldn't run in this session's sandbox (typecheck is clean; your CI runs it on push), and the NestJS 10→11 upgrade in `UPGRADE.md` is still worth doing before go-live.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 07:06

Two different sources: the top one comes **from iKhokha**, the four URLs are **yours** (things you host/define).

**From the iKhokha Merchant Dashboard** — sign in, go to **Payments → iK Pay API**, and generate your keys. That screen gives you the three credentials:

- `IKHOKHA_APP_ID` — the **API Key / Application ID** (`IK-APPID`)
- `IKHOKHA_APP_SECRET` — the **API Secret** (used to sign requests)
- `IKHOKHA_ENTITY_ID` — the **entityID** (the "Application key ID" shown alongside the keys)

You'll need a live iKhokha merchant account to see these; there's usually a test/sandbox mode too, so do your first transaction in test mode.

**The four URLs are your own app's endpoints** — you decide them (just swap `example.com` for your real domain):

- `IKHOKHA_CALLBACK_URL` — **your API's webhook**, server-to-server. iKhokha POSTs the payment result here. This one already exists in your code: `https://api.<yourdomain>/api/payments/webhook/ikhokha`. It must be publicly reachable (it will be, behind Caddy).
- `IKHOKHA_SUCCESS_URL` / `IKHOKHA_FAIL_URL` / `IKHOKHA_CANCEL_URL` — **browser redirect pages**. After paying, iKhokha sends the shopper's browser to one of these. They're just landing pages in your web app.

The catch: those three success/fail/cancel pages **don't exist yet** — `/pay/success`, `/pay/failed`, `/pay/cancelled` are placeholders I put in the example. For a first deploy you can point all three at any real page (even `https://app.<yourdomain>/`), but it's a rough experience.

Want me to build the three `/pay/*` landing pages in the web console (branded, with a "back to dashboard" / "retry payment" action)? It's quick and makes the payment loop feel finished. I'd also recommend I cross-check the exact request field names (`requesterUrl`, `mode`, `externalTransactionID`) and the callback signature against iKhokha's official examples before you go live — I can do that against their GitHub samples.

Sources: [iK Pay API overview (developer.ikhokha.com)](https://developer.ikhokha.com/overview), [iK Pay API product page](https://www.ikhokha.com/ik-pay-api), [iKhokha official API examples (GitHub)](https://github.com/ikhokha/ik-pay-api-examples)

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 07:49

Done — inbound iKhokha callback signature verification is in, opt-in and unit-tested. Everything compiles clean (backend `src` + the spec).

**What I added:**
- **`IkhokhaPaymentProvider.verify(path, rawBody, secret, provided)`** — recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 over the callback path + raw body and compares it to the `IK-SIGN` header with a **timing-safe** equality check.
- **Webhook handler** now verifies when `IKHOKHA_VERIFY_CALLBACK=true`: it reads the **exact raw bytes** (`req.rawBody`, which your app already captures via `rawBody: true`), signs over the callback URL's pathname, and returns **401** on a mismatch (logged). Left **off by default** so it can't reject real callbacks before you've confirmed iKhokha's inbound signing format.
- **Env flag** `IKHOKHA_VERIFY_CALLBACK` added to `.env.example`, `deploy/.env.prod.example`, and both compose files (default `false`).
- **Three tests**: a correctly-signed callback passes; a tampered body fails; a wrong/absent signature fails.

**How you turn it on (after your first real callback):**
1. Do a sandbox transaction and capture the callback iKhokha sends — confirm it includes an `IK-SIGN` header and that it's HMAC over `path + body` (vs body-only, or a different path).
2. If it matches, set `IKHOKHA_VERIFY_CALLBACK=true` and redeploy — spoofed callbacks are now rejected.
3. If their inbound scheme differs, tell me the shape and I'll adjust the one `verify()` helper (it's isolated on purpose).

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 08:25

DNS is **not** managed on Contabo — it's set wherever your domain's nameservers point, which is almost always the **registrar you bought the domain from** (or a DNS host like Cloudflare if you moved it there).

**How to find the right place:**
1. Log in to whoever you registered the domain with — common SA/global registrars: Afrihost, domains.co.za, Xneelo/Hetzner (the web host, not the VPS), GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare.
2. Find the section called **DNS**, **DNS Management**, **Zone Editor**, **Advanced DNS**, or **Nameservers**.
3. Add two **A records**:

| Type | Name / Host | Value | TTL |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `app` | `169.58.46.223` | Auto / 300 |
| A | `api` | `169.58.46.223` | Auto / 300 |

(Some panels want just `app`; others want the full `app.yourdomain.com`. The "Value"/"Points to" is always your VPS IP, `169.58.46.223`.)

**Two gotchas:**
- **Cloudflare users:** set each record's proxy status to **DNS only (grey cloud)**, at least until Caddy has issued its Let's Encrypt certs — the orange-cloud proxy interferes with that. (You can turn it back on afterward if you configure Cloudflare's origin/SSL properly.)
- Propagation takes a few minutes to a couple of hours. Check with `dig app.yourdomain.com +short` — once it returns `169.58.46.223`, you're good to `docker compose up` so Caddy can fetch the certificate.

You're on the SendGrid integration screen — you don't actually need to pick a language here. Our code already talks to SendGrid; you just need to **create an API key** and **verify a sender**. Here's exactly what to do:

**2. Verify a sender** (SendGrid won't deliver until the "from" address is verified)
- **Settings** → **Sender Authentication**.
- Easiest for now: **Single Sender Verification** → **Create New Sender** → use an address you can receive mail at (e.g. your own inbox, or `no-reply@dantalan.co.za` if you have that mailbox). SendGrid emails a confirmation link — click it.
- Whatever address you verify must match `SENDGRID_FROM` in your `.env.prod`.
- (The more robust option is **Domain Authentication** for `dantalan.co.za` — adds DNS records so all `@dantalan.co.za` addresses work — but single sender is fine to launch.)

```dotenv

SENDGRID_API_KEY=«redacted»        # the key from step 1
SENDGRID_FROM=<the exact address you verified in step 2>
```

- If you verify your own personal inbox as the sender for now, set `SENDGRID_FROM` to that exact address (not `no-reply@dantalan.co.za`) — an unverified "from" will bounce.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 10:44

You don't need any — Postgres and Redis run as **containers in your own stack**, and you *create* their credentials rather than getting them from somewhere.

Here's how it works:
- **Postgres**: the compose file spins up a Postgres container with user `pms`, database `pms`, and the password **you set** in `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`. So whatever you put there *becomes* the password — it's not looked up anywhere. Just generate a random one.
- **Redis**: runs with **no password** (it's only reachable inside the private Docker network, never exposed to the internet), so there's nothing to set.

The app connects to them internally via the compose file, which builds the connection strings for you:
```
DATABASE_URL = postgres://pms:«redacted»@postgres:5432/pms
REDIS_URL    = redis://redis:6379
```
That's why `DATABASE_URL`/`REDIS_URL` aren't in your `.env.prod` — they're derived automatically.

**So the only thing you do** is set `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` to a fresh random value. On the VPS:

```bash
openssl rand -hex 24
```

Copy that output into `deploy/.env.prod`:
```dotenv
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=«redacted» hex string you just generated>
```

Use the **hex** value (letters/numbers only) — don't invent one with `@`, `:`, or `/` in it, because those characters would break the `DATABASE_URL`.

That's the last required secret. Once your `.env.prod` has:
- `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` (generated) ✓
- `JWT_SECRET` + `PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (generated) ✓
- `SENDGRID_API_KEY` + verified `SENDGRID_FROM` ✓
- `IKHOKHA_APP_SECRET` (the regenerated one) ✓

…you're ready to build. Save the file (`Ctrl+O`, Enter, `Ctrl+X`) and run:
```bash
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build
```

- **Caddy**: `certificate obtained successfully` for `app.dantalan.co.za`/`api.dantalan.co.za` = TLS is live. If it keeps retrying, DNS hasn't fully propagated yet.

Don't run migrations yet — do that in step 11 once the API container is up.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 10:54

That's a build error, not config — everything else (API image, DB, Redis, Caddy) is fine. The web build failed on the very last step because **there's no `web-admin/public/` folder**, and the Dockerfile tries to copy it:

```
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public   →   "/app/public": not found
```

Two fixes — do the quick one on the VPS now to unblock, and I'll also fix it in the repo permanently.

**Immediate (on the VPS)** — create the empty folder, then rerun the build:
```bash
mkdir -p web-admin/public && touch web-admin/public/.gitkeep
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build
```

That's all it needs — Next.js just doesn't emit a `public/` when you have no static files, and the Dockerfile assumed one exists.

Let me also add it to the repo so it never happens again (CI, future rebuilds):

The DB role setup worked (`pms_app ready`). The migration failed for a real reason: the **production image only contains compiled `dist/` + prod dependencies** — but `npm run migration:run` uses `ts-node` against the TypeScript source, and `ts-node`/`tsconfig-paths` are dev-only and not in the image. It needs to run against the compiled data-source instead.

**Run this instead (works right now, no rebuild):**

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec api node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:run -d dist/common/database/data-source.js
```

That invokes the TypeORM CLI (which *is* in the image, since typeorm is a runtime dep) against the compiled `dist/…/data-source.js`, whose migrations live in `dist/…/migrations/*.js`.

All fixed in the repo. Now let's roll it out correctly. Because your app image bakes `package.json` and the DB connection is changing, this needs a `git pull` + rebuild.

**On your PC** (PowerShell):
```powershell
cd C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3
git add -A
git commit -m "Prod: app connects as pms_app (RLS enforced), owner-based migrations, web public dir"
git push
```

**On the VPS:**
```bash
cd ~/PMS03
rm -f web-admin/public/.gitkeep    # remove the manual placeholder so the pull isn't blocked
git pull
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec api npm run migration:run:prod
```

What changed and why:
- The **app now connects as `pms_app`** (RLS enforced) via `DATABASE_URL`, while **migrations run as the `pms` owner** via a separate `MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL` — the new `migration:run:prod` script automatically uses the owner URL to create tables, then the app uses the restricted role at runtime.
- The rebuild picks up the new `package.json` (so `npm run migration:run:prod` exists in the image) and recreates the API container with the two DB URLs.

Then verify:
```bash
curl https://api.dantalan.co.za/api/health/ready
```
Expect `{"status":"ok","checks":{"database":"up","redis":"up"}}`, and https://app.dantalan.co.za still loads.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 11:09

Branch mismatch — the giveaway is `main -> origin/main` updated but "Already up to date" for your checkout. Your **PC pushed to `main`**, but the **VPS is still on `chore/nest-11`**, so the rebuild used the old `package.json` without the `migration:run:prod` script.

Fix: move the VPS onto `main` (which now has everything), then rebuild:

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
git checkout main
git pull origin main
grep migration:run:prod package.json    # sanity check — should print the two lines
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec api npm run migration:run:prod
```

If `git checkout main` complains about an untracked `web-admin/public`, run `rm -rf web-admin/public` first, then retry — the tracked version comes back with the branch.

From now on, **stay on `main`** on both your PC and the VPS so this doesn't recur — `main` is your source of truth. (The `chore/nest-11` branch has served its purpose; you can delete it later with `git branch -d chore/nest-11` locally and on GitHub.)

Once `migration:run:prod` completes cleanly (you'll see TypeORM logging each migration as it applies), verify:
```bash
curl https://api.dantalan.co.za/api/health/ready
```

Then we bootstrap your first agency + admin login so you can actually sign in. Paste the migration output and I'll confirm you're good.

Found the mechanism. The app only uses SendGrid **if `SENDGRID_API_KEY` is present in the container at boot** — otherwise it silently falls back to a console stub that "succeeds" but sends nothing (and the OTP endpoint always returns 200 to prevent email enumeration, so the UI gives no error either way). Two usual culprits: the key isn't actually in the container, or the container wasn't recreated after you added it.

Run these three on the VPS:

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
# 1. Is the key actually inside the running api container?
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec api printenv | grep -iE "SENDGRID|OTP_CHANNEL"

# 2. Which email provider did it pick at boot? (want: SendGridEmailProvider)
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod logs api 2>&1 | grep -i "channels —" | tail -3

# 3. Now request a fresh code on the login page, then immediately:
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod logs api --tail 40 2>&1 | grep -iE "otp|sendgrid|notify|mail|deliver|error"
```

How to read the results:

- **No `SENDGRID_API_KEY` in step 1** → it's missing from `deploy/.env.prod` (or the container predates it). Add it, then recreate: `docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d api`.
- **Step 2 shows `email:EmailProvider`** (not `SendGridEmailProvider`) → the key wasn't set when the container started. Same fix: recreate the api container.
- **Step 2 shows `email:SendGridEmailProvider` but still nothing** → the send is being rejected. Step 3 will show `sendgrid 401` (bad/insufficient key — the API key needs **Mail Send** permission) or `sendgrid 403` (from-address not verified — your `SENDGRID_FROM` **must be exactly `pms@dantalan.co.za`**, your verified single sender).

Paste the three outputs and I'll tell you the exact fix.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 12:14

Same OTP mechanism for everyone — the manual SQL was only needed for *you* because the database was empty and someone had to be the first owner. From here on, nobody is created by hand.

**The flow is identical for every user:** they go to their app, enter their email, receive a 6‑digit code from `pms@dantalan.co.za`, and enter it. What differs is only *what they can see after login*, which comes from their **membership** (role + scope).

**How each type gets a membership** — created automatically by staff actions inside the app, not by SQL:

- **Tenants** — created when you approve a rental application / set up a lease. The code get‑or‑creates their user by email and gives them a `tenant` membership (`ensureTenantUser`). They then log into the **tenant app**.
- **Owners** — added in the Owners section; they get owner access to the **owner portal** (web) / landlord app.
- **Service providers** — added in the Providers section; they get a `service_provider` membership.
- **Extra staff** (property managers) — added as memberships on your vendor; they log into the **web back‑office**.

So the rule is: **the person's record must exist first** (staff creates it). If someone enters an email that has no membership, they'll authenticate but land with no agency/role — an empty account. That's exactly the empty state your first login would've had before the bootstrap.

Two practical notes:

- **Phone/SMS OTP isn't live yet.** Only email is wired (SendGrid). SMS falls back to a console stub that delivers nothing. If tenants will log in by phone number, you need to add Twilio creds (`TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID`, `TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN`, `TWILIO_FROM`) and recreate the api container.
- **SendGrid trial has a daily send cap** (~100 emails/day). Fine for testing; upgrade the plan before real tenant volume. Your domain is authenticated so deliverability is good.

One thing worth flagging for later: every OTP email currently sends from `pms@dantalan.co.za` regardless of which agency the user belongs to. Fine while Dantalan is the only vendor, but for true white‑label you'd eventually want a per‑vendor sender address/domain. ### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 14:08

That "Unauthorized" means your **current login token carries no owner role** — every action on this page requires `vendor_owner`. The most likely cause: you logged in as `talandan26@gmail.com` *before* the email change applied, so the OTP flow auto-created a **new, membership-less** user with that email. Because `users.email` is unique, the later `UPDATE` (vernon → talandan26) would then have hit a conflict and changed nothing — leaving your owner membership stranded on the old `vernon` user.

This one block reconciles it no matter which state you're in — it ensures the `talandan26` user holds the `vendor_owner` membership on your Dantalan vendor:

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms <<'SQL'
DO $$
DECLARE v_vendor uuid; v_target uuid;
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO users (name, email, status)
  VALUES ('Dan Talane', 'talandan26@gmail.com', 'active')
  ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

  SELECT id INTO v_target FROM users WHERE email = 'talandan26@gmail.com';

  SELECT vendor_id INTO v_vendor FROM memberships WHERE role = 'vendor_owner'
    ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1;
  IF v_vendor IS NULL THEN
    SELECT id INTO v_vendor FROM vendors WHERE name = 'Dantalan Properties'
      ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1;
  END IF;

  INSERT INTO memberships (vendor_id, user_id, role)
  VALUES (v_vendor, v_target, 'vendor_owner')
  ON CONFLICT (vendor_id, user_id) DO UPDATE SET role = 'vendor_owner';
END $$;

SELECT u.email, m.role, m.vendor_id FROM users u
  JOIN memberships m ON m.user_id = u.id ORDER BY u.email;
SQL
```

The final table should show `talandan26@gmail.com` with `role = vendor_owner`.

Then the important part: **sign out and sign back in.** Your current token was minted without the role, so fixing the database won't upgrade it — you need a fresh OTP login to get a token that carries `vendor_owner`. After that, "Add property" will work.

Paste the output table if anything looks off (e.g. two users, or the role still missing).

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 14:14

Perfect — that's a clean picture. Your membership is now correct (owner of **Dantalan Properties** only), and the junk is small: a **Rivonia Rentals** seed vendor (created 11:01, before your bootstrap) plus its seed users, and **zero** properties/leases. So the purge is safe and simple.

This removes the Rivonia vendor, all its vendor-scoped rows (across every table automatically), and any now-orphaned seed users — while leaving Dantalan and your account untouched. It disables FK checks for the transaction so delete-order can't trip us up:

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms <<'SQL'
BEGIN;
SET session_replication_role = replica;   -- disable FK enforcement for the cleanup

DO $$
DECLARE r record; v uuid := 'd0ba90ad-44b2-4f11-958f-a29dde838bac';
BEGIN
  -- delete every vendor-scoped row belonging to Rivonia, in any table
  FOR r IN
    SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.columns
    WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND column_name = 'vendor_id'
  LOOP
    EXECUTE format('DELETE FROM %I WHERE vendor_id = $1', r.table_name) USING v;
  END LOOP;

  DELETE FROM vendors WHERE id = v;

  -- remove users with no memberships left (the seed accounts; your admin keeps Dantalan)
  DELETE FROM users u WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM memberships m WHERE m.user_id = u.id);
END $$;

SET session_replication_role = DEFAULT;
COMMIT;

-- Confirm final state:
SELECT id, name FROM vendors;
SELECT u.email, m.role, v.name AS vendor
FROM users u LEFT JOIN memberships m ON m.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN vendors v ON v.id = m.vendor_id
ORDER BY u.email;
SQL
```

Expected result: **one vendor** (Dantalan Properties) and **one user** (`talandan26@gmail.com` → `vendor_owner` → Dantalan Properties). Nothing else.

Both apps **already guard web** — token storage falls back to `localStorage` on web (`isWeb ? localStorage : SecureStore`), so `expo-secure-store` (which throws on web) is never called in the browser build. ### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-21 14:29

Both apps are wired to be hosted as web URLs. Here's everything I added/changed:

- `mobile-tenant/Dockerfile` + `mobile-landlord/Dockerfile` — build the Expo web export, serve it with Caddy on `:80`, API base baked in at build time.
- `web.Caddyfile` + `.dockerignore` in each app.
- `deploy/Caddyfile` — new TLS routes for `tenant.` and `landlord.dantalan.co.za`.
- `deploy/compose.prod.yml` + `compose.prod.images.yml` — new `tenant`/`landlord` services (reusing your existing `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE`), and Caddy now depends on them.

No new env vars needed — the apps reuse `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE` (`https://api.dantalan.co.za/api`).

**Step 1 — Add DNS records** (at your DNS provider for dantalan.co.za), same as your existing app/api records:

```
A   tenant     169.58.46.223
A   landlord   169.58.46.223
```
(optional IPv6: `AAAA tenant` and `AAAA landlord` → `2a02:c207:2345:3343::1`)

**Step 2 — Push the code** (from your dev machine workspace):

```bash
git add mobile-tenant mobile-landlord deploy
git commit -m "Serve tenant & landlord apps as hosted web (Expo web export + Caddy)"
git push origin main
```

**Step 3 — Build & bring them up on the VPS:**

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
git pull origin main
# Build the two web bundles (takes a few minutes each the first time)
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build tenant landlord
# Reload Caddy so it picks up the new routes and fetches certs
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d caddy
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod ps
```

**Step 4 — Verify** once DNS has propagated:

```bash
curl -I https://tenant.dantalan.co.za
curl -I https://landlord.dantalan.co.za
```

Expect `HTTP/2 200`. Then open **https://tenant.dantalan.co.za** and **https://landlord.dantalan.co.za** in a browser — tenants/landlords log in with the same email-OTP flow (their user must exist first, e.g. a tenant created via a lease).

Two notes: DNS must resolve before Caddy can issue the certs (it'll retry automatically for a minute or two), and the apps currently load the default theme (`VENDOR_SLUG='demo'`) — branding per-subdomain is a later enhancement. If a build fails on the VPS, paste the output and I'll fix it.

Want me to also set up **Twilio SMS login** next, or wire the apps to pull your Dantalan branding?

What I changed: each app (tenant, landlord, web back-office) now derives the brand key from its hostname — `tenant.dantalan.co.za` → `dantalan.co.za` — and fetches that theme, falling back to the `dantalan` slug off-web (native builds). The backend already resolves that via `vendors.custom_domain`.

**Step 1 — push (dev machine):**

```bash
git add mobile-tenant mobile-landlord web-admin
git commit -m "Resolve white-label branding per-subdomain from hostname"
git push origin main
```

**Step 2 — on the VPS: pull, tag the vendor + store the charcoal+gold theme:**

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
git pull origin main
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms <<'SQL'
UPDATE vendors SET
  slug = 'dantalan',
  custom_domain = 'dantalan.co.za',
  config = COALESCE(config, '{}'::jsonb) || jsonb_build_object('branding', '{
    "tagline": "Property management, done right.",
    "logo": { "text": "Dantalan Properties" },
    "colors": {
      "brand": "#23272F", "onBrand": "#ffffff", "tint": "#F4EEDD", "accent": "#C9A227",
      "ink": "#16181D", "muted": "#6B7280", "line": "#E6E7EA", "bg": "#F6F6F5", "card": "#FFFFFF",
      "danger": "#A23A26", "dangerBg": "#F7ECE7", "success": "#2F7D5A"
    },
    "font": { "family": "System", "headingFamily": "System" },
    "contact": { "email": "pms@dantalan.co.za", "website": "dantalan.co.za" }
  }'::jsonb),
  updated_at = now()
WHERE name = 'Dantalan Properties'
RETURNING id, name, slug, custom_domain;
SQL
```

You should see one row with `slug = dantalan`, `custom_domain = dantalan.co.za`. Verify the endpoint resolves:

```bash
curl https://api.dantalan.co.za/api/branding/dantalan.co.za
```

That should return the Dantalan brand JSON (charcoal `#23272F`, gold `#C9A227`, "Dantalan Properties").

**Step 3 — rebuild the three front-ends:**

```bash
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d --build web tenant landlord
```

Then hard-refresh (Ctrl-Shift-R) app / tenant / landlord.dantalan.co.za — all three should show the charcoal + gold Dantalan brand and wordmark.

You can fine-tune colours, tagline, and upload a logo anytime in the web back-office under **Settings → Branding**; changes flow to all three apps automatically. Once you've confirmed it looks right, paste the `curl` output or a screenshot and I'll mark this done — or tell me and I'll tweak the palette.

No code change needed — the API already enforces an explicit allowlist from `CORS_ORIGINS`, and yours is still set to only `https://app.dantalan.co.za`. So the API correctly refuses the `tenant.`/`landlord.` origins. Just widen the allowlist and restart the API (it's a runtime env var — no rebuild):

```bash
cd ~/PMS03
sed -i 's|^CORS_ORIGINS=.*|CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.dantalan.co.za,https://tenant.dantalan.co.za,https://landlord.dantalan.co.za|' deploy/.env.prod
docker compose -f deploy/compose.prod.yml --env-file deploy/.env.prod up -d api
```

Wait ~10s for the API to come back, then hard-refresh (Ctrl-Shift-R) the landlord app and request the OTP again. The branding fetch and `otp/request` will now return the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header and succeed.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-22 09:01

Here's the honest picture: there's **no single "Add tenant" button** in the back-office today. Tenants are onboarded through the **leasing funnel**, and the tenant's login account is created automatically when you **approve** them. The designed flow is:

1. **Properties** → add a property and its **unit(s)**.
2. **Listings** → create a listing for a vacant unit and **Publish** it.
3. An **application** comes in against that listing (name, email, phone).
4. **Applications** → optionally **Screen**, then **Approve & create lease** (you pick the start date). Approving does three things automatically: creates the tenant's **user + tenant membership** (by email), creates the **lease** on the unit, and marks the unit occupied.
5. The tenant then logs in at **tenant.dantalan.co.za** with that email (OTP) and sees their lease.

The gap: step 3 (submitting the application) is a **public endpoint** with no staff-facing form in the UI — it's meant for a public listings site you haven't built yet. So right now you can't complete the whole thing by clicking alone; you'd submit the application via the API, then Approve in the UI. For example, once a listing is published:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.dantalan.co.za/api/listings/applications \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"listingId":"<LISTING_ID>","applicantName":"Jane Tenant","applicantEmail":"jane@example.com","applicantPhone":"+27..."}'
```

…then go to **Applications → Approve**.

That's clunky for a real agency. What you almost certainly want is a proper **"Add tenant" action** in the back-office — one form (tenant name/email/phone, unit, rent, start date) that creates the tenant account and the lease directly, skipping the listing/application dance. All the backend pieces exist (`ensureTenantUser` + `createLease`); it just needs an endpoint and a button.

Want me to build that "Add tenant" feature? I'd add a staff endpoint plus a button on the Leases (or Properties) page so you can onboard a tenant to a unit in one step. Otherwise I can walk you through the listing-based flow end to end.

Here's the single sequence that ships everything still pending — branding (per-subdomain) + Add-tenant + the CORS fix — in one pass.

**1. Commit & push everything (dev machine):**
