### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-30 09:39

Typecheck is clean. The flow is now gated correctly.

What changed:

On approval, the applicant's tenant membership is created as **`pending`** instead of active. The login lookup (`auth_memberships_for_user`) now only returns **active** memberships, so a pending applicant resolves to no vendor context and cannot enter the tenant app — even though their user record and lease exist. When they open the signing link and complete the lease, `complete()` flips their membership to **active**, unlocking access.

The emails now match the flow:
- **Approval email** — congratulates them and points to the one required next step: "Review & sign your lease" (plus "View your move-in invoice"). No portal sign-in link, since there's no access yet. This is now a single email — the lease agreement's separate sign-link email is suppressed on the approval path so the applicant gets one clear message.
- **Lease-signed confirmation** — now says the portal is ready with a "Sign in to your portal" button.

Staff-initiated direct onboarding (`addTenant`) is unchanged — it still grants active access immediately, since that's a deliberate staff action. Existing memberships all default to `active`, so no one currently in the system loses access.

This one **needs a migration**. Deploy:

```
cd <repo>   # the dir containing deploy/compose.prod.yml
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T api npm run migration:run:prod
```

One note on the between-state: a pending applicant who tries to log in will receive an OTP but land with no accessible data (no vendor context) — access is simply closed until they sign. If you'd prefer they instead see an explicit "please sign your lease first" message at login, I can add that as a follow-up.

To stage and commit everything remaining (tracked modifications + new untracked files) in one go:

```
git add -A && git commit -m "your message here"
```

`git add -A` stages all changes across the whole repo (modifications, new files, and deletions); `-m` sets the commit message. If you'd rather only include already-tracked files and skip untracked ones, use `git commit -am "your message"` instead.

On the VPS (in the repo dir that contains `deploy/compose.prod.yml`):

```bash
git pull

```

If the `caddy reload` errors (e.g. Caddyfile isn't at that path), just recreate the container instead — it picks up the mounted file:

```

```bash

  psql -U pms -d pms -c "UPDATE vendors SET custom_domain='dantalan.co.za' WHERE slug='dantalan';"
```

2. DNS: apex `@` and `www` A-records already point to `169.58.46.223`, so nothing new is needed there. Only add an `about` A-record if you want the marketing site live at `about.dantalan.co.za` (it's moved off the apex).

The `Address` it returns must be **169.58.46.223** (your Contabo VPS). Expect a `301/302/308` redirect to `/rentals`. If you see that, the server is fine and it's purely the A-record. If instead you get an error or the wrong content there, the Caddyfile/containers still need attention and we debug that path.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 03:39

Before we design repos and servers, the most important reframe: **this project is already a multi-tenant, white-label platform.** Dantalan isn't the app — it's one `vendor` row. Branding, custom domains, RLS isolation, the partner/reseller portal, and subscription tiers are all already built. So "a white-label version called Locare" can mean two very different things, and which one you mean decides everything downstream:

**Option 1 — Locare is the platform brand.** Locare becomes the neutral name of the SaaS itself, the thing you sell to property agencies. Dantalan becomes "agency #1" living on it. `locare.co.za` is the storefront + signup + platform-admin; each agency runs at `{agency}.locare.co.za` or their own domain (exactly like `dantalan.co.za` already does). Nothing gets forked — you add a platform-brand layer and onboard agencies as vendors. Your partner portal and subscription billing *are* the monetisation engine for this.

**Option 2 — Locare is a separate, isolated instance.** Same code, but a physically separate stack (own VPS, own DB, own domain) for a different operator or market, fully walled off from the Dantalan world. Useful if you want to sell "the whole platform" to another operator, or need hard billing/data separation.

My strong recommendation is **Option 1 with Option 2 as a later escape hatch**, because the codebase was built for it and forking would create drift you'll regret.

Here's how each layer looks under that recommendation:

**Repo.** One repo, never a fork. All per-brand differences live in (a) the `vendors` table (colours, logo, custom_domain) and (b) environment config for anything platform-wide. If you ever need a truly separate instance, it's the *same repo* deployed twice with different `deploy/.env.prod` + Caddyfile — not a code copy.

**What's genuinely new for Locare.** A *platform-level* brand (today branding is per-vendor only) — the chrome shown on `locare.co.za` itself: the marketing site, the agency signup flow, and the default when no vendor domain matches. Plus a platform-admin surface (you already have `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS` and admin pages) to approve/create agencies.

**VPS / DB.** Start with the single VPS you have: Locare + Dantalan + every future agency share one stack, one Postgres, isolated by RLS. That's the cheapest and simplest, and it's what's running now. You only split to a second VPS / separate DB when a specific client demands physical isolation or you outgrow one box — and because it's the same repo, that's a deploy concern, not a rewrite.

**Domains.** Already solved: `public_listings` and `public_branding` resolve by `slug OR custom_domain`, and the front-end derives the brand from the hostname. Onboarding an agency = insert a vendor, set its slug + optional custom_domain, add DNS. We literally just did this for Dantalan.

**Billing.** Locare charges agencies via the subscription tiers; agencies charge their tenants via the existing rent/invoice engine; resellers earn via the partner commission system. All present.

To turn this into a concrete plan, I need three decisions:

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 04:01

Sure — here's what each one actually means and why it matters.

**1. Wildcard TLS — how HTTPS certificates get issued for agency subdomains.**

Every `{agency}.locare.co.za` needs a valid HTTPS certificate or browsers show a security warning. There are two ways to get them:

- *DNS-01 wildcard cert*: you obtain a single certificate for `*.locare.co.za` that covers every possible subdomain at once. To prove you own the domain, Caddy has to create a temporary DNS record automatically, which means giving Caddy an API token for wherever your DNS is hosted (via a Caddy DNS-provider plugin). Upside: one cert covers unlimited agencies instantly, no per-agency issuance step. Downside: you must wire up the DNS-provider plugin and store a DNS API token.
- *On-demand TLS per subdomain*: Caddy issues a separate certificate the first moment each subdomain is first visited. Upside: no DNS token needed. Downside: the very first visit to a new agency is slightly slow while the cert mints, and it doesn't cover wildcards as cleanly — plus you'd want the "ask" gate working perfectly to avoid abuse.

Note: your agency *custom domains* (like `dantalan.co.za`) will use on-demand TLS regardless — that part isn't optional. This question is only about the `*.locare.co.za` subdomains. I lean DNS-01 wildcard because it's tidier at scale, provided you're comfortable adding a DNS API token.

**2. Mobile apps — one app for all agencies, or one per agency.**

You have Expo tenant and landlord apps. On the web, a single app already serves every agency (it figures out which agency from the domain). Mobile is different because an app is installed from a store, not visited by URL:

- *Single shared apps*: one "Tenant" app and one "Landlord" app in the stores. The user logs in and the app figures out which agency they belong to from their account. Upside: one app to build, ship, and maintain; new agencies need no app work. Downside: the app is Locare-branded, not per-agency — an agency can't have "Dantalan" in the App Store.
- *Per-agency apps*: each agency gets their own branded app in the stores. Upside: fully white-label, agency's name/icon on the phone. Downside: enormous overhead — a separate store listing, build, and review cycle per agency, forever.

I strongly lean single shared apps; per-agency native apps rarely pay off unless a big agency specifically demands it.

**3. The Locare apex (`locare.co.za`) — pure marketing, or also a combined listings portal.**

`locare.co.za` itself (not an agency subdomain) has to show *something*. Two visions:

- *Pure marketing + signup*: the apex is the sales site — "here's the platform, sign your agency up." Renters never go there; they go to a specific agency's site. Simple and on-brand for a SaaS.
- *Aggregate meta-portal*: the apex also shows a combined feed of rentals from *all* agencies (like a Property24 / mini-portal), so a renter can browse everything Locare-powered in one place, then get routed to the relevant agency to apply. Upside: it becomes a consumer destination that drives traffic and leads to your agencies — a real selling point. Downside: more to build (cross-vendor public search, dedup, ranking), and some agencies may not want their stock pooled with competitors, so you'd need an opt-in flag.

This one's a genuine product/strategy call rather than a technical one: is Locare purely "software you sell to agencies," or also "a rental marketplace that agencies plug into"? The marketplace angle is more ambitious but potentially far more valuable.

Want me to record your answers into the design doc, or talk through any of these further before deciding?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 04:10

There's no HostAfrica plugin for Caddy — the `caddy-dns` ecosystem covers Cloudflare, Linode, GoDaddy, etc., but not HostAfrica, and DNS-01 wildcard needs a plugin that can talk to your DNS provider's API. So DNS-01 directly against HostAfrica isn't possible. Two clean ways around it:

**Option A — move DNS for `locare.co.za` to Cloudflare (recommended).** Keep the domain registered at HostAfrica; just change its nameservers to Cloudflare (free tier). Then use the well-maintained `caddy-dns/cloudflare` plugin with a scoped API token. This is the standard, reliable path and gives you fast DNS + easy management as a bonus. Your existing `dantalan.co.za` custom-domain flow (on-demand TLS) is unaffected.

**Option B — ACME-DNS delegation (keep DNS at HostAfrica).** Run a small `acme-dns` service and add one `_acme-challenge.locare.co.za` CNAME at HostAfrica pointing to it; Caddy uses the `caddy-dns/acmedns` plugin. Keeps everything at HostAfrica but adds a service to run and a bit more setup.

My recommendation is A — the Cloudflare plugin is first-class and it's a five-minute nameserver change. Let me record that in the doc.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-31 04:13

For Q2 - if a agency did want their own mobile app how complex would it be to build?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 04:14

Genuinely not much *engineering* — the hard part is app-store logistics, not code. Because your Expo tenant and landlord apps are already white-label and pull branding (colours, logo, name) from the API at runtime, a per-agency app is mostly a packaging-and-publishing exercise, not a rebuild.

Here's where the effort actually sits, lightest to heaviest:

**Code/config — low.** You'd add a build-time config so an app is pinned to one agency (its vendor/slug and API base) instead of resolving by login, plus per-agency `app.config.js` values: app name, icon, splash, bundle identifier (iOS) / package name (Android), and a deep-link scheme. Expo handles this cleanly with dynamic config + `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` env, so one codebase produces N branded builds. A day or two to set the pattern up the first time; minutes per agency after that.

**Build pipeline — medium, but one-time.** You'd set up EAS Build profiles (Expo's cloud build) so each agency build is reproducible with its own identifiers and assets. Once the pattern exists it's a parameterised job.

**App Store / Play Store — this is the real cost, and it's ongoing.** Each app needs a store listing (screenshots, description, privacy policy, support URL) and passes review. The important catch: Apple's guideline 4.3 actively rejects near-identical "template" apps submitted under a single developer account. The accepted path for white-label is that **each agency publishes under their own Apple ($99/yr) and Google ($25 once) developer accounts** — you build and upload, they own the listing. That means per-agency credentials, review cycles, and coordination. Budget the first agency app at a few days end-to-end (mostly waiting on review and gathering assets), faster after.

**Maintenance — the quiet tax.** Every SDK bump, OS change, or new feature has to be rebuilt and re-submitted across every agency app, each with its own signing keys and store credentials. Ten agency apps is roughly ten times the release overhead of one shared app.

So my recommendation for the doc: **default everyone to the single shared Locare apps**, and offer a per-agency native app as a **premium / Enterprise add-on** — published under the agency's own developer accounts, priced to cover the setup and ongoing release work. And in the meantime, note that the web app can be a **PWA** ("Add to Home Screen"): each agency's branded site becomes an installable, icon-on-the-homescreen app with no store submission at all — that covers most of what agencies actually want (a branded icon on tenants' phones) for near-zero incremental cost.

Want me to record Q2 as "shared apps by default; per-agency native as a paid Enterprise add-on; PWA as the cheap middle option" in the design doc?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 07:31

Caddyfile now has Locare's routes. Here's the full deploy — do these in order.

**1. Commit & push (Windows)**
```powershell
Remove-Item C:\xampp\htdocs\development\PMS0.3\.git\*.lock -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
git add .
git commit -m "Locare marketing page + brand SVGs + locare.co.za routes"
git push
```

**2. DNS at HostAfrica** — add three A records, all → `169.58.46.223`:
- `@` (locare.co.za)
- `www`
- `api`

Caddy issues TLS certs via HTTP-01 for these exact hostnames, so no DNS plugin is needed here (the `*.locare.co.za` wildcard for agencies is the later DNS-01 work). Give DNS a few minutes to resolve before step 4.

**3. Allow the lead form's origin** — on the VPS, edit `deploy/.env.prod` and append the Locare origins to `CORS_ORIGINS` (the marketing form on `locare.co.za` POSTs to `api.locare.co.za`):
```
...,https://locare.co.za,https://www.locare.co.za
```

**4. Deploy (on the VPS)**
```bash
git pull
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build marketing
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --force-recreate api caddy
```

`--build marketing` ships the new page; recreating `api` reloads the CORS change; recreating `caddy` picks up the new Caddyfile and starts fetching the `locare.co.za` certs.

Then visit `https://locare.co.za` — it should load the Locare page with your SVG logo, and the "Start your agency" / partner forms should submit successfully.

One note: the lead form points at `https://api.locare.co.za/api/leads`. If you'd rather not add the `api` record yet, tell me and I'll switch the form back to `api.dantalan.co.za` (same backend) so you only need the `@` and `www` records.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 07:42

Good news: two of the three are already done. Your apex `@` A-record points to `169.58.46.223`, and `www` is a CNAME to `locare.co.za`, so it resolves to the VPS too — both `locare.co.za` and `www.locare.co.za` are ready for Caddy.

The only missing one is **`api.locare.co.za`**, which the lead form calls. Add one record:

- **Name:** `api`
- **Type:** `A`
- **RDATA:** `169.58.46.223`
- **TTL:** `14400` (default is fine)

(A CNAME `api → locare.co.za` would also work, but a plain A record is cleaner for an API host.)

Once that's in, all three hostnames resolve to the VPS and the deploy steps I gave will get Caddy to issue certs for each.

Alternatively, if you'd rather not add the `api` record right now, say so and I'll point the marketing form back at `api.dantalan.co.za` (same backend) — then you don't touch DNS at all, since apex + www already work. Your call.

One unrelated heads-up I noticed: you have an `MX 0 locare.co.za` plus an SPF TXT — that's your email setup and is fine; nothing to change there for this deploy.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 10:58

`talandan26@gmail.com` already exists as a user in the DB, so you can't just rename Vernon's account onto it. Instead, transfer the ownership to that existing user. This block handles both cases — whether `talandan26` already has a membership in the Dantalan vendor or not — and makes it the active owner:

```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms <<'SQL'
DO $$
DECLARE v_vendor uuid; u_old uuid; u_new uuid;
BEGIN
  SELECT id INTO v_vendor FROM vendors WHERE slug='dantalan';
  SELECT id INTO u_old FROM users WHERE email='vernon@zaaka.io';
  SELECT id INTO u_new FROM users WHERE email='talandan26@gmail.com';

  IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM memberships WHERE vendor_id=v_vendor AND user_id=u_new) THEN
    -- talandan26 is already in this vendor: promote to active owner
    UPDATE memberships SET role='vendor_owner', status='active'
      WHERE vendor_id=v_vendor AND user_id=u_new;
    DELETE FROM memberships
      WHERE vendor_id=v_vendor AND user_id=u_old AND role='vendor_owner';
  ELSE
    -- move Vernon's owner membership onto talandan26
    UPDATE memberships SET user_id=u_new, status='active'
      WHERE vendor_id=v_vendor AND user_id=u_old AND role='vendor_owner';
  END IF;
END $$;
SQL
```

After this, `talandan26@gmail.com` is the Dantalan owner and signs in with that address; Vernon's user row stays but no longer owns the agency.

Confirm it worked:

```bash

```

You should see `talandan26@gmail.com` as `vendor_owner` / `active`. The public **contact** email is separate — run the `vendors.config` update I gave earlier if you also want that changed.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-07-31 13:13

let's brainstorm a chatbot on the Locare marketing page to answer FAQs

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 13:14

Good one — and worth thinking through before building, because a marketing chatbot has a sharp accuracy/cost tradeoff. Here's the landscape and where I'd land.

The key constraint: the Locare marketing page is a **static** site (plain HTML in the `marketing` container). So the bot's "brains" can live in one of two places, and that choice drives everything:

**Front-end only (scripted).** A curated set of Q&As baked into the page's JS. The user clicks a question chip or types, we keyword-match, and return a canned answer. Zero cost, zero latency, no backend, no hallucination, fully on-brand. But rigid — it only answers what you anticipated, and free-text phrasing it hasn't seen falls through.

**Backend (Claude-powered).** A small endpoint on your existing NestJS API (`/api/faq-chat`) takes the question, injects a tightly-scoped Locare knowledge base as context, calls Claude, and returns a grounded answer. Natural, handles any phrasing, feels premium. Costs per message, needs the `api.locare.co.za` route + CORS (which you're already setting up), and needs guardrails so it never invents pricing or wanders off-topic. You already have an LLM provider abstraction in the codebase (from the lease-parser work), so this reuses existing plumbing.

My recommendation is a **hybrid**: a floating Locare-blue bubble that opens with 4–6 suggested question chips (instant, free, scripted for your most common FAQs), plus a free-text box that falls through to the Claude endpoint for anything else. Every answer ends with a soft "still want to chat? book a demo" that drops into your existing lead form — so the bot is also a lead funnel, not just a help desk.

Three things I'd bake in regardless:
- **Grounding + guardrails.** One curated `FAQ`/knowledge file is the single source of truth; the system prompt tells Claude to answer *only* from it and to say "I'm not certain — let me connect you" (→ demo form) otherwise. No made-up pricing, no off-topic answers. Use Claude Haiku — cheap and fast enough for FAQs.
- **Abuse/cost control.** It's a public endpoint, so: per-IP rate limit, a max messages-per-session cap, and a token ceiling. Otherwise a bored visitor (or a bot) runs up your bill.
- **POPIA note.** A one-line "chats may be processed to answer you; don't share sensitive info" disclosure, and only capture an email when the visitor volunteers one for a callback.

A sensible build order: ship the **scripted** version first (it's a self-contained front-end change, live today, no API/DNS dependency), then layer the Claude endpoint on once `api.locare.co.za` is up.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 13:41

That error means Caddy is answering on 443 but can't present a valid certificate for `locare.co.za` — almost always because Caddy isn't running the updated Caddyfile yet (so there's no site block for the host, and it can't get a cert), or cert issuance is failing. Let me pin it down on the VPS.

**1. Is the Locare block actually inside the running Caddy container?**
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec caddy \
  sh -c 'grep -nE "locare|on_demand|:443" /etc/caddy/Caddyfile'
```

- If this prints **nothing** for `locare`, Caddy is still on the old config — pull and force-recreate it:
  ```bash
  git pull
  docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --force-recreate caddy
  ```
- If it shows an `on_demand` line or a bare `:443`, that's the cause (on-demand TLS with no working `ask` endpoint fails the handshake → this exact error). It shouldn't be there — the committed Caddyfile only has named `locare.co.za` blocks. Tell me and I'll help you reconcile it.

**2. Watch the certificate issuance in the logs:**
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml logs --tail=150 caddy \
  | grep -iE "locare|acme|challenge|obtain|certificate|error"
```

Look for either `certificate obtained successfully` (good — just wait ~30s and reload) or an ACME error explaining the failure.

Two common issuance blockers to check while you're there:
- **Port 80 must be open and reachable** from the internet (Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 hits it). Dantalan's certs work, so it usually is — but confirm nothing changed.
- **Don't keep refreshing/retrying** — Let's Encrypt rate-limits repeated failures (5/hour/host). If you've hit it, Caddy will keep failing for up to an hour even once the config is right.

Paste the output of steps 1 and 2 and I'll tell you the exact fix.

That's a DNS error — "Server Not Found" means `app.locare.co.za` doesn't resolve to any server, so the browser never even reaches the VPS. The `app` A-record hasn't been created (or hasn't propagated yet).

Check it on Windows:
```powershell
nslookup app.locare.co.za
```
If it says "can't find" / Non-existent domain, the record's missing.

Add it at **HostAfrica** (same place you added the others):
- **Name:** `app`
- **Type:** `A`
- **RDATA:** `169.58.46.223`
- **TTL:** `14400`

(A CNAME `app → locare.co.za` works too, since `locare.co.za` already points to the VPS.)

Give it a few minutes to propagate, then `nslookup app.locare.co.za` should return `169.58.46.223`, and the site will load. First hit over HTTPS, Caddy will fetch the cert (needs the `app.locare.co.za` Caddy route deployed — which it is if you pushed and recreated `caddy`).

This is purely the missing DNS record — nothing wrong on the server side. Once `nslookup` shows the VPS IP, you're good.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 16:29

Correct — and it's working as designed, not a bug. What you're seeing depends on **two independent things**:

- **Branding follows the hostname.** `app.locare.co.za` → Locare theme, always, no matter who logs in. That part is right (you can see the Locare wordmark + blue).
- **The navigation/content follows your role.** You signed in as `vernon@zaaka.io`, who is a **platform admin** — so you get Locare's *operator console* (Partners, Commissions, Billing): the tools for running the platform and managing agencies. A platform admin has no vendor context, so there are no properties/listings/rent to show — that's why the nav is short.

The full property-management back office (Dashboard, Properties, Listings, Payments, Reports, etc.) belongs to **agency users** (owner / property manager), and it's scoped by RLS to their agency's data. It's the *same app* — it just renders that richer nav when the logged-in user is an agency member.

So to see exactly what you're expecting — "the app.dantalan.co.za back office, but Locare-branded" — sign in at `app.locare.co.za` as an **agency user**, e.g. `talandan26@gmail.com` (the Dantalan owner). You'll get:
- the full agency nav + Dantalan's data (RLS-scoped to that vendor), and
- the Locare theme, because branding is host-based.

In short: platform admin = the small operator console (what you saw); agency login = the full back office. Both live in the same app on `app.locare.co.za`.

One design note worth flagging: an agency user logging in at `app.locare.co.za` will see *Locare* branding rather than their own — which is fine for you testing/supporting, but in normal use each agency would work from their own subdomain/custom domain (like `app.dantalan.co.za`) to get their own brand. If you eventually want platform admins to be able to *drop into* a specific agency's back office (support/impersonation) from the Locare console, that's a separate feature I can spec — just say the word.

Spec'd and queued. The design doc is at `docs/LOCARE_ADMIN_IMPERSONATION_DESIGN.md`, and I've added five tasks (#188–#192) covering the build in order:

- **#188** — backend core: `/admin/impersonate` + `/stop`, the `act` JWT claim, vendor-scoped revocable token with a TTL.
- **#189** — audit trail: `impersonation_events` table + start/stop logging + admin read endpoint.
- **#190** — web enter flow: "Open back office →" on the agencies list, token swap, redirect into the agency dashboard.
- **#191** — the persistent "Viewing {Agency} as Locare support · Exit" banner + exit flow.
- **#192** — admin audit view + full verification (guards, TTL, revocation, RLS scoping) and deploy.

The design leans on what's already there: because the RLS interceptor scopes everything by the token's `vendorId`, impersonation is mostly "mint a vendor-scoped token for the admin with an `act` marker" — no per-endpoint rework. Locked the safe defaults (platform-admin only, one agency at a time, time-boxed + revocable, audited, Locare theme + naming banner), and parked read-only mode, agency-notify/consent, and agency-brand view as later enhancements.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 16:51

Those two errors point at different layers, so let's separate them:

- **"Forbidden resource"** is a `403` from the API — a role guard rejected the request. That happens when the logged-in user has **no usable role** (empty roles / no active vendor membership), so every role-guarded endpoint refuses it.
- **"Failed to fetch"** is a browser network-level failure (CORS or connectivity), *not* a 403.

Since `vernon@zaaka.io` logged in fine on the same `app.locare.co.za`, CORS for that origin is already working — so the most likely story is that `dantalan98@gmail.com` simply **has no active agency membership**, lands with an empty role, and gets forbidden on the dashboard's data calls (with a secondary fetch failing as a knock-on).

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 18:41

"NetworkError when attempting to fetch" on that form means the browser can't reach the endpoint it posts to — `https://api.locare.co.za/api/leads`. Two usual culprits: `api.locare.co.za` doesn't resolve/serve HTTPS yet, or CORS is blocking the `locare.co.za` origin. Let's check both.

**1. Does `api.locare.co.za` actually resolve and serve HTTPS?**

On Windows:
```powershell
nslookup api.locare.co.za
```
It must return `169.58.46.223`. If it says "can't find / non-existent", the `api` A-record was never added — add it at HostAfrica (Name `api`, Type `A`, `169.58.46.223`). Caddy already has the `api.locare.co.za` route, so once DNS resolves it'll fetch a cert.

Then confirm the API answers on that host (run anywhere):
```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://api.locare.co.za/api/branding/dantalan
```
`200` = the API host is live. Anything else (or a TLS/connection error) = DNS/cert not ready.

**2. Does CORS allow the marketing origin?** On the VPS:
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec api printenv CORS_ORIGINS
```
That must contain `https://locare.co.za` **and** `https://www.locare.co.za` (the page's origin). If not, add them to `deploy/.env.prod` `CORS_ORIGINS` and reload:
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --force-recreate api
```

My bet is one of these two: the `api.locare.co.za` A-record isn't in yet, or `locare.co.za` isn't in `CORS_ORIGINS`.

If you'd rather not add the `api` record at all, I can point the marketing forms at `api.dantalan.co.za` (which already resolves) instead — you'd still need `https://locare.co.za` in `CORS_ORIGINS`. Tell me which way you want to go, and paste the `nslookup` + `curl` + `CORS_ORIGINS` output if it's not obvious.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-07-31 19:12

The form reports success because the `/leads` endpoint saves the lead and returns `200` *regardless* of whether the notification email actually sends — email is a separate, silent path. So the lead is almost certainly stored; the email just didn't land. The logs will tell us exactly why.

**1. See what the notify actually did** (on the VPS):
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml logs --tail=150 api | grep -iE "lead|notify|sendgrid"
```
Read it like this:
- `lead notify failed: sendgrid 4xx …` → SendGrid rejected the send (usually an unverified sender or a bad recipient).
- The lead body just printed with no send → the email channel wasn't used.
- Nothing about a lead at all → the new routing code isn't running (see #3).

**2. Confirm the lead was stored and what type it is:**
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms -c "SELECT type, name, email, created_at FROM leads ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;"
```
You want to see a recent row with `type = agent`.

**3. Make sure the new code is actually deployed.** The partner-routing change is *code* (`leads.service.ts`) — a `--force-recreate` (which you did for CORS) reloads env but does **not** rebuild code. Rebuild it:
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec api printenv PARTNER_NOTIFY_EMAIL
```

**4. The mailbox must exist.** Since `locare.co.za`'s MX points to HostAfrica, `partners@locare.co.za` has to be a real mailbox there to receive — if it was never created, SendGrid sends and it bounces into the void. Create it in HostAfrica (or, quick test, temporarily point `PARTNER_NOTIFY_EMAIL` at a Gmail you can check).

Most likely it's a combination: the code wasn't rebuilt (so it used the old `LEADS_NOTIFY_EMAIL`), and/or `partners@locare.co.za` isn't a live mailbox yet. Paste the log grep + the `leads` query output and I'll tell you which.

One aside worth knowing: OTP sign-in emails are reaching you, so SendGrid itself and your `SENDGRID_FROM` sender are working — which points the finger at the recipient mailbox or the code-not-rebuilt, not SendGrid.

## 2026-08-01

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-08-01 05:51

I want to switch to social media(google) login - is this a good move. give me pros and cons

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-01 05:52

Short answer: adding Google login is a solid win for the agency/admin side, but **replacing** OTP entirely — especially for tenants — would likely hurt you. Here's the balanced view.

**Pros**

- **Faster, higher-conversion sign-in.** One tap, no waiting for a code, no typos, no "check your spam." That matters most for agency signup and staff.
- **Sidesteps your current email-deliverability pain.** You're actively fighting SendGrid/spam issues right now; Google login removes email OTP from the critical path for anyone who uses it.
- **Verified email for free**, and password security is entirely Google's problem (you already have no passwords with OTP, so this stays clean).
- **Less support load** — no "I didn't get my code" tickets.

**Cons**

- **Tenants are the risk.** In South Africa a lot of renters live on phone/WhatsApp and non-Google email. Making Google the *only* way in would lock out a chunk of your tenant base — and tenants must reach their portal to pay rent and sign leases. Your **SMS OTP** channel is genuinely valuable here; Google is email-only.
- **White-label friction.** A "Sign in with Google" button puts Google's branding on an agency's own-domain site — it slightly breaks the "this is *my* platform" illusion you're selling.
- **Custom domains + OAuth is fiddly.** Google OAuth needs each redirect URI registered. With agencies on their own domains (`dantalan.co.za`, etc.) and wildcard `*.locare.co.za`, you'd have to centralise auth on one domain (e.g. `auth.locare.co.za`) and redirect back — real added complexity versus your current host-agnostic OTP.
- **Account-linking edge cases.** Someone who applied via email OTP and later clicks Google must resolve to the *same* user; mismatched emails create duplicates.
- **New dependencies:** OAuth consent-screen verification, a published privacy policy, POPIA consent for sharing data with Google, and B2B agencies who use Microsoft rather than Google.

**My recommendation:** don't rip out OTP — **add Google as an additional option**, targeted where it pays off:

- Agency signup + staff + platform admin (B2B): Google login is a great fit and eases your email woes.
- Tenants (B2C): keep email **and SMS** OTP as the primary path; offer Google as a convenience, not a requirement.

That gives you the conversion/UX upside without excluding phone-first tenants or complicating your white-label/custom-domain story. If you want, I can spec exactly that — Google OAuth via a central `auth.locare.co.za`, account-linking rules, and keeping OTP as fallback — and add it to the todo.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-01 06:13

Google login is built and both backend and web typecheck clean — implemented as an **additive** option (OTP untouched), off by default.

What's in place:
- **Backend:** `users.google_sub` + migration; `GoogleOAuthService` (authorize URL, code exchange, id-token decode + `iss`/`aud`/`exp`/`email_verified` validation); the four account-linking rules (match sub / link empty / reject conflict / create); `/auth/google/{enabled,start,callback,exchange}` with throttling; a signed `state` carrying the return origin (validated against `CORS_ORIGINS` to block open redirects) and a single-use one-time code so the token never rides in a URL. OTP and Google now share one `issueForUser()` (same membership resolution, pending-lease handling, revocable session).
- **Web:** a "Continue with Google" button on the login screen (only shows when enabled) and an `/auth/google/return` page that exchanges the code and routes by role; new users with no membership flow into the `/no-access` screen.
- **Infra:** it reuses the existing `api.locare.co.za` as the single fixed redirect host — **no new subdomain/DNS needed**.

Tasks #194–#196 are done; **#197 stays open** for the POPIA consent line + privacy link on the button, tests, and the Google Cloud setup.

To turn it on (safe to deploy first — the button stays hidden until configured):

1. **Google Cloud** → create an OAuth 2.0 Web client; Authorized redirect URI = `https://api.locare.co.za/api/auth/google/callback`; configure the consent screen (scopes `openid email profile`) + privacy-policy URL.
2. **`deploy/.env.prod`:**
   ```
   GOOGLE_OAUTH_ENABLED=true
   GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=...
   GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=...
   AUTH_BASE=https://api.locare.co.za
   ```
   and make sure `CORS_ORIGINS` includes every app origin you'll sign in from (`https://app.locare.co.za`, `https://app.dantalan.co.za`, …).
3. **Deploy:**
   ```bash
   git pull
   docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api web
   docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T api npm run migration:run:prod
   ```

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-01 06:45

Two of those you set yourself; two come from Google. Here's the split:

- **`GOOGLE_OAUTH_ENABLED=true`** — you set this. It's just the on/off switch for the feature. Leave it `false` until the Google client is ready.
- **`AUTH_BASE=https://api.locare.co.za`** — you set this. It's already the correct value (your API host). Don't change it.
- **`GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`** and **`GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`** — these you create in the **Google Cloud Console**. Here's how:

**1. Create/select a project** — go to [console.cloud.google.com](https://console.cloud.google.com), and in the top project picker create a project (e.g. "Locare") or pick an existing one.

**2. Configure the OAuth consent screen** — APIs & Services → **OAuth consent screen** (in newer console it's under "Google Auth Platform → Branding"):
- User type: **External**.
- App name: `Locare`; user support email; app logo (optional).
- App domain / authorized domain: `locare.co.za`.
- Privacy policy URL + Terms URL (can be simple pages on `locare.co.za`).
- Scopes: add **`openid`, `.../auth/userinfo.email`, `.../auth/userinfo.profile`** — these are non-sensitive, so no Google verification review is required.
- While testing, either add your own Google account under **Test users**, or click **Publish app** to go live.

**3. Create the OAuth client** — APIs & Services → **Credentials** → **Create credentials** → **OAuth client ID**:
- Application type: **Web application**.
- Name: e.g. `Locare web`.
- **Authorized redirect URIs** → add exactly:
  `https://api.locare.co.za/api/auth/google/callback`
- Click **Create**.

Google then shows you a **Client ID** and **Client secret** — those are your `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`. (You can reopen the client later to copy them again.)

Then put all four into `deploy/.env.prod`, redeploy `api`/`web`, and the "Continue with Google" button appears.

Two gotchas that trip most people up:
- The redirect URI must match **character-for-character** — `https`, `api.locare.co.za`, and the `/api/auth/google/callback` path exactly, no trailing slash.
- If you leave the consent screen in **Testing** mode, only accounts listed as test users can sign in; **Publish** it for anyone to use.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-01 07:32

First — **don't restart, recreate, `docker compose up`, or reboot anything.** The running containers still hold every secret in memory, and that's your recovery source. A recreate right now would both fail (the compose file requires those vars) and lose your only copy. So freeze the server as-is.

Good news: `.env.prod` is fully reconstructable from the running containers.

**1. Confirm it's gone and find your container names:**
```bash
ls -la deploy/.env.prod
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}'
```
(You should see `deploy-api-1`, `deploy-postgres-1`, etc. — adjust names below if they differ.)

**2. Rebuild the file from the live container env.** This uses plain `docker exec` (not `docker compose exec`), so it works even though the env file is missing:
```bash
{
  echo "# Recovered $(date -u) from running containers"
  echo "POSTGRES_PASSWORD=«redacted» exec deploy-postgres-1 printenv POSTGRES_PASSWORD)"
  echo "NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE=$(docker exec deploy-api-1 printenv PUBLIC_API_BASE)"
  docker exec deploy-api-1 printenv | grep -vE '^(PATH|HOME|HOSTNAME|TERM|PWD|SHLVL|OLDPWD|NODE_VERSION|YARN_VERSION|_|npm_|MEDIA_DIR|PUBLIC_API_BASE|POSTGRES_PASSWORD)='
} > deploy/.env.prod
```

**3. Review it** against the template to make sure nothing's missing:
```bash
cat deploy/.env.prod
diff <(grep -oE '^[A-Z_]+' deploy/.env.prod.example | sort -u) <(grep -oE '^[A-Z_]+' deploy/.env.prod | sort -u)
```
The `diff` shows any keys the example has that your recovered file doesn't. `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE` are handled explicitly above; anything else missing, tell me and we'll source it.

**4. Verify compose can read it (does NOT recreate anything):**
```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml config >/dev/null && echo "env file OK"
```
`env file OK` means every `${VAR:?}` required value is present.

**5. Back it up so this can't bite again:**
```bash
cp deploy/.env.prod ~/env.prod.backup
```

Why the running containers are enough: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` must match what Postgres already stored on its volume (recovering the live value avoids locking yourself out of the DB), and `JWT_SECRET` plus all the SendGrid/payment/Google keys are sitting in the api container's environment right now. Reconstruct, verify with step 4, *then* it's safe to deploy again.

Paste the `cat` / `diff` output if you want me to sanity-check it before you carry on.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 08:34

The impersonation feature is the "sign in as agency" support tool we spec'd earlier (tasks #188–#192, design doc at `docs/LOCARE_ADMIN_IMPERSONATION_DESIGN.md`). It's not built yet — just designed and queued.

In plain terms: it lets a **Locare platform admin** (you) open a specific agency's back office to see exactly what that agency sees — their Dashboard, Properties, Listings, Payments, etc. — so you can help troubleshoot without needing the agency's own login.

It came out of your earlier question about `app.locare.co.za`: as a platform admin you only see the operator console (Partners / Commissions / Billing), because an admin has no agency data of their own. Impersonation is the bridge — a controlled way to step into a chosen agency's view.

How it's designed to work, and the guardrails that make it safe:

- From an **Agencies list** in the admin console, you click "Open back office" on an agency. The system mints a token scoped to that one agency (reusing the RLS engine, so all their data is scoped correctly), tagged with an "acting as" marker.
- A persistent, distinctly-coloured **banner** shows "Viewing {Agency} as Locare support · Exit" so it's never mistaken for normal use, and one click returns you to the admin console.
- It's **platform-admin only**, **one agency at a time**, **time-boxed** (auto-expires, ~45 min) and **instantly revocable**, and every start/stop is written to an **audit log** (who, which agency, when, how long, optional reason) that you can review.
- PII/banking stays encrypted and masked exactly as for a normal agency user — impersonation grants a role's *view*, nothing more. MVP is full read/write; a read-only support mode is noted as a later enhancement.

Think of it as the "log in as this customer to help them" button that most SaaS support tools have, but built with an audit trail and time limits so it's accountable.

It's split into five tasks: backend core (#188), audit trail (#189), the web "enter" flow (#190), the banner/exit (#191), and the audit view + verification (#192). Want me to build it now, or was this just to refresh what it is?

Both files are type-safe. The code path itself was correct — the real question is *which* of three things is happening in production, and the old code was silent on success so you couldn't tell. Now it logs the outcome explicitly.

```

```

On the VPS:

```
git pull
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api

Then submit one test partner registration on the site, and check what the api logged:

```
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml logs --tail=40 api | grep -i "lead notify\|channels —"
```

That one line tells us exactly where it's breaking:

- **"no email channel configured"** → `SENDGRID_API_KEY` isn't reaching the container. Fix: add it to `.env.prod`, redeploy.
- **"lead notify failed → …: sendgrid 403"** → `SENDGRID_FROM` isn't a verified sender. Fix: verify that sender (or authenticate the domain) in SendGrid.
- **"lead notify sent → partners@locare.co.za (…message-id…)"** → SendGrid *accepted* it, so it's a deliverability problem — the mail is landing in spam or being filtered by HostAfrica. This is the most likely case, and the fix is DNS.

If it's the third (most probable), the durable fix is domain authentication in SendGrid so HostAfrica trusts the mail:

1. In SendGrid → Settings → Sender Authentication → **Authenticate Your Domain** for `locare.co.za`.
2. SendGrid gives you ~3 CNAME records — add them to `locare.co.za` DNS at HostAfrica.
3. Set `SENDGRID_FROM` to an address on that domain (e.g. `no-reply@locare.co.za`), redeploy.
4. Add/confirm an SPF record including SendGrid and let DKIM (the CNAMEs) validate.

Paste me the log line from the test submission and I'll tell you exactly which fix applies.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 10:45

Yes — there's a clear problem, and it's almost certainly the exact thing HostAfrica is fixing.

Your **MX and `mail` records point at the domain apex, which now resolves to your Contabo VPS, not HostAfrica's mail server:**

- `MX @ → 0 locare.co.za`
- `A @ → 169.58.46.223` (the VPS)
- `CNAME mail → locare.co.za` (→ also the VPS)

So mail for anything `@locare.co.za` is being routed to `169.58.46.223`, which runs your app, not a mail server. That's a classic split-hosting break: you repointed the apex `A` record to the VPS for the website, and HostAfrica's default "mail follows the apex" pattern got dragged along with it. The mailbox `partners@locare.co.za` lives on HostAfrica's mail server (their SPF shows it at `169.239.180.4` / `spf.host-ww.net`), but the MX no longer points there — so inbound mail to the partner inbox is misrouted.

This affects the fix we just built in two ways:

1. **Inbound**: even a perfectly-sent email to `partners@locare.co.za` won't land in the HostAfrica inbox while MX points to the VPS.
2. **Outbound SMTP**: `SMTP_HOST=mail.locare.co.za` would connect to the VPS (no mail server there), so that value won't work as-is.

What HostAfrica needs to do (and likely is):

- Point **MX** to their mail server, e.g. `mail.locare.co.za` **priority 10** (not the apex).
- Make **`mail`** an `A` record to their mail-server IP (the `169.239.180.x` / host-ww.net side), **not** a CNAME to `locare.co.za`.
- Ideally add a **DKIM** record (`default._domainkey` TXT) — I don't see one — and optionally `_dmarc`.

Your SPF is otherwise fine and already authorizes HostAfrica's relay (`+mx`, `include:spf.host-ww.net`, `ip4:169.239.180.4`), so once MX/`mail` point back to HostAfrica, our SMTP-relay approach is SPF-aligned and will deliver.

Two things to confirm with them so I can finish #193: the exact **SMTP hostname** to use for `SMTP_HOST` (once `mail.locare.co.za` resolves to their server, that's the value), and that `MX`/`mail` are repointed. The `api` and `app` A records → VPS are correct; leave those.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 10:50

Here are the exact steps. You're only changing **two records** (`mail` and `MX`) and optionally adding DKIM. Leave everything else (`@`, `api`, `app`, `www`, `NS`, `SOA`, and the SPF `TXT`) exactly as-is.

**Step 1 — Get your mail server details from HostAfrica hosting**

In the HostAfrica panel go to **Web Hosting → open the hosting package for locare.co.za → cPanel**. Then:

- Open **Email Accounts**, find `partners@locare.co.za`, click **Connect Devices** (or "Set Up Mail Client"). Note the **Incoming/Outgoing server hostname** (something like `mailXX.host-ww.net`) and the ports.
- On the cPanel home page, note the **Shared IP Address** (right-hand "General Information" panel). That's your mail server IP — it should be on the `169.239.x.x` range, matching the `169.239.180.4` already in your SPF.

**Step 2 — Fix the `mail` record** (it currently points to your VPS)

- On the DNS page, find the row `mail | CNAME | locare.co.za` and click **Delete**.
- Click **+ Add DNS Record** and create:
  - Type: **A**
  - Name: **mail**
  - TTL: **3600**
  - RDATA / Address: **the Shared IP from Step 1** (the `169.239.x.x` mail-server IP)

**Step 3 — Fix the MX record** (it currently routes mail to your VPS)

- Find the row `@ | MX | 0 locare.co.za` and click **Edit**.
- Set **Priority: 10** and **Target/RDATA: `mail.locare.co.za`** (so it reads `10 mail.locare.co.za`), TTL 3600, and save.

**Step 4 — Add DKIM (recommended, improves deliverability)**

- In cPanel open **Email Deliverability**. For `locare.co.za`, if DKIM shows as missing or "Repair", click **Repair** (HostAfrica usually adds it automatically), or copy the DKIM `TXT` record it shows and add it here via **+ Add DNS Record** (Type TXT, the Name/value they give). Keep your existing SPF unchanged.

**Step 5 — Verify (after ~15–30 min for propagation)**

From your PC:

```
nslookup -type=mx locare.co.za
nslookup mail.locare.co.za
```

MX should return `mail.locare.co.za`, and `mail.locare.co.za` should resolve to the `169.239.x.x` IP (not `169.58.46.223`). Then send a test email **from an outside account (e.g. your Gmail) to partners@locare.co.za** — it should land in the HostAfrica inbox.

**Step 6 — Then point the app's SMTP at it** (once Step 5 passes)

On the VPS, in `.env.prod`:

```
SMTP_HOST=mail.locare.co.za      # or the mailXX.host-ww.net hostname from Step 1
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=partners@locare.co.za
SMTP_PASS=«redacted»
SMTP_FROM=partners@locare.co.za
```

Then redeploy `api` and run the test partner registration.

The single most important change is **Step 3** — until MX points to `mail.locare.co.za` (on HostAfrica's IP) instead of the apex, mail keeps going to your VPS. If cPanel won't show a Shared IP on the `169.239.x.x` range, tell me what it shows and I'll adjust.

That profile confirms the exact mail settings HostAfrica expects:

- **Server (incoming & outgoing): `mail.locare.co.za`**
- **Username: `partners@locare.co.za`** (the full address)

Once `mail.locare.co.za` resolves to the HostAfrica IP, these are your confirmed app SMTP values:

```
SMTP_HOST=mail.locare.co.za
SMTP_PORT=465
SMTP_SECURE=true
SMTP_USER=partners@locare.co.za

(Port 465 with SSL matches the profile. If HostAfrica prefers 587, use `SMTP_PORT=587` and leave `SMTP_SECURE` blank — the provider auto-negotiates STARTTLS.)

The partner portal is part of your back-office web app, at **`app.locare.co.za`** — you reach it by logging in with an email that's registered as a partner. Here's the full path:

So if the same email is also in `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS`, it'll open the *admin* portal, not the partner one. To see the partner portal, use an email that's a partner member but **not** a platform admin.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-08-04 12:14

I think Twilio & SendGrid are not cost effective at this point I want to create a custom user creation path when a tenant is approved. Let's brainstorm.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 12:15

Good instinct — and worth noting you've already removed most of the cost: the HostAfrica SMTP path makes **email effectively free** (it's bundled with your hosting), so email OTP/invites cost you nothing once DNS propagates. The expensive piece is really SMS (Twilio). So the question splits into two: how tenants get their *first* login, and what channel you lean on.

Here's the landscape.

**The core design choice: one email forever, or an email every login.**

Your auth today is passwordless OTP — every login sends a code, so delivery cost recurs forever. The most cost-effective shift is an **activation invite + password**: on approval you send *one* email with a link to set a password, and from then on the tenant logs in with email + password — zero delivery cost per login. Passwordless is nice UX but only "free" because your SMTP is now free; a password means you're not dependent on delivery at all after day one.

**How the invite reaches the tenant (in order of cost):**

- *Email magic/activation link via HostAfrica SMTP* — free. "Your [Agency] account is ready → set your password." This is the default and covers most tenants.
- *Staff-mediated link* — after approval, the back office shows a **copy-able activation link + short claim code**. Staff paste it into WhatsApp or read the code to the tenant. Zero infrastructure, works when a tenant has no reliable email, and WhatsApp is near-universal in SA.
- *Cheaper SA SMS gateway* — if you want automated SMS, swap Twilio for a local provider (SMSPortal, BulkSMS, Clickatell) at roughly R0.20–0.35/SMS vs Twilio's international rates. Same OTP flow, much lower cost, only if you truly need automated SMS.

**Where it hooks in.** You already flip tenant membership to *active* on lease signing (that work's done). The "custom creation path" is really the **credential-delivery / activation step** layered on top of that event — approve/lease-sign fires → generate a signed, single-use, time-boxed activation token → surface it as (a) an emailed link and (b) a copy-able link + code in the back office.

**My recommended default:** activation-link email via HostAfrica SMTP as the automated path, *plus* a "copy invite link / code" button in the approval screen as the always-works fallback — and drop Twilio entirely for now. Google login stays as a third option for tenants who have Gmail. That gets you to zero variable cost while still automated for the common case.

Three things shape the build, so tell me:

1. Do tenants reliably have **email**, or should WhatsApp/copy-link be the primary channel?
2. **Password** accounts (one delivery ever) or keep **passwordless** (free now via SMTP, simpler for tenants)?
3. Fully **automated** on approval, or **staff-mediated** (staff send the link themselves)?

Where do you land on those, and I'll turn it into a concrete spec?

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-08-04 12:21

1. both and whatsapp must be the primary channel  - 2. keep passwordless 3.Full automated.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 12:22

That's a clean set of constraints. Let me lay out the concrete design, then flag the one real prerequisite.

**The shape of it**

Login stays passwordless — no passwords, OTP each login. What changes is the delivery layer: a **channel cascade** with WhatsApp primary, email fallback, both fully automated. Every system message (login OTP *and* the tenant-approved welcome) goes: try WhatsApp → if it fails or there's no WhatsApp-capable number, fall back to HostAfrica email. Twilio/SendGrid get dropped entirely.

**On approval (automated)**

Your tenant membership already flips to *active* on lease signing. We hook that event to enqueue a `TENANT_WELCOME` message over the cascade: a WhatsApp message "Your [Agency] tenant account is ready — open the app and sign in with this number/email." Because login is passwordless, there's no credential to deliver — the welcome just points them to the tenant app, and their first login sends an OTP over the same cascade.

**WhatsApp, done cost-effectively**

The cheap, no-Twilio route is Meta's **WhatsApp Cloud API directly** (you pay Meta per conversation, no reseller markup — much cheaper than Twilio SMS, and open rates in SA are far higher). It slots into your existing `ChannelProvider` interface as a new `whatsapp` channel — a thin Graph API HTTP provider, same pattern as the SendGrid/SMTP ones.

**The one prerequisite you can't skip:** automated WhatsApp requires a Meta setup — a WhatsApp Business Account, a dedicated sender number, a permanent access token, and **pre-approved message templates** (one "authentication" template for the OTP code, one "utility" template for the welcome). Business-initiated messages *must* use approved templates; that's a Meta rule, not ours. Template approval usually takes a few hours to a day. Until that's done, the cascade just uses email.

**Cost lever worth building in:** since passwordless means an OTP per login, we add "remember this device" (longer trusted session) so tenants aren't triggering a WhatsApp message every single login — keeps the per-login cost near zero for returning users.

The design doc is in your repo at `docs/LOCARE_WHATSAPP_ONBOARDING_DESIGN.md`.

The headline on cost: going **Meta Cloud API direct**, your only variable cost is per-message, and everything fixed (platform fee, verification, templates, email fallback) is **R0**. A realistic run at ~200 tenants lands around **R1,000/year** — driven almost entirely by login OTPs at roughly **R0.14–0.25 each** (SA domestic authentication rate), with the welcome message negligible and email fallback free. Two levers keep it there: register the WhatsApp Business Account **in South Africa** (domestic rate ≈ R0.20 vs international ≈ R0.50), and the remember-this-device session so returning tenants don't fire an OTP every login.

Two things to flag: all Meta rates are estimates at ~R18/$1 and are reviewed quarterly, so confirm on Meta's rate card before committing — and from **1 October 2026** utility/service messages inside the service window start being charged, which nudges the welcome-message line up a little. Both are noted in the doc.

The build is designed to ship safely email-only first (nothing breaks while `WHATSAPP_TOKEN` is blank), and WhatsApp switches on automatically once your Meta templates are approved.

Want me to start building #198–#201 now?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 12:44

Built #198–#201 (and #203 is covered by the design doc). No new dependencies and no migration — WhatsApp uses `fetch`. What went in:

- **WhatsApp Cloud provider** (`http.providers.ts`) — Meta Graph API, template messages, auth copy-code button; only active when `WHATSAPP_TOKEN` + `WHATSAPP_PHONE_ID` are set.
- **Channel cascade** (`cascade.ts`) — tries channels in order, stops at first success; wired into OTP delivery and the tenant welcome. Default `whatsapp,email`.
- **E.164 normalisation** (`e164.ts`) — applied at tenant creation and phone login so numbers are canonical for WhatsApp.
- **Automated welcome** — the lease-signing `complete()` now sends the welcome over the cascade instead of email-only.
- **Env validation** updated to be cascade- and SMTP-aware (it previously would have failed prod boot on email-without-SendGrid).

It ships safe: with `WHATSAPP_TOKEN` blank, everything runs **email-only** and behaves exactly as before.

Verify on Windows (only the known `sharp` line should show):

```
npx tsc -p tsconfig.build.json --noEmit
npx jest e164 cascade
```

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 12:50

Build succeeded and the API is up. The grep just missed — the em-dash in the log line doesn't match a plain `—` in all terminals, and 30 lines may not reach startup. Try:

```
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml logs api | grep -iE "channels|whatsapp|Notify"
```

You're looking for a line like `channels ... email:SmtpEmailProvider ... whatsapp:off`. Whatever it shows for `email:` and `whatsapp:` tells us the interim state — `whatsapp:off` is expected and correct until your Meta token is set.

If that still returns nothing, just confirm the container is healthy and serving:

```
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml logs --tail=40 api
```

The deploy itself worked — the new code (cascade, E.164, WhatsApp provider, automated welcome) is now live and running email-only, exactly as intended. Paste whatever the channels line shows and I'll confirm, then we can move on to the Meta setup or #202 whenever you're ready.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 14:59

That's exactly right:

`email:SmtpEmailProvider sms:TwilioSmsProvider push:PushProvider whatsapp:off`

The cascade is live and running email-only through your HostAfrica SMTP — `whatsapp:off` because the Meta token isn't set yet, which is the correct interim state. Once your DNS finishes propagating, OTPs and the tenant welcome will deliver over SMTP; when you complete the Meta setup and set `WHATSAPP_TOKEN`, WhatsApp becomes primary automatically with no code change.

One thing worth noting: `sms:TwilioSmsProvider` means Twilio credentials are still in your env. It's harmless (SMS isn't in the cascade, so it's never called), but you can drop `TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID` from `.env.prod` whenever you want to fully retire it.

#198–#201 are done and deployed. What's left in this thread:

- **#202 remember-this-device** — the cost-saver so returning tenants don't trigger a WhatsApp OTP every login. Pure backend, buildable now.
- **Meta setup** — your side (WABA in SA, sender number, token, template approval), per §8 of the design doc.

Want me to build #202 now, or leave it until WhatsApp is actually switched on?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 15:10

#202 is built end-to-end (backend + web-admin reference client). No new deps, no migration.

What it does: on OTP verify with **"Remember this device"** ticked (default on), the server returns a 30-day device token stored client-side. On next launch the app calls `/auth/device/login` and silently re-auths — **no OTP sent**, so no WhatsApp/SMS cost for returning users. The token is hashed server-side, **rotated on every use** (single-use, so a captured token can't be replayed), revoked on sign-out, and tunable via `TRUSTED_DEVICE_DAYS` (0 disables). The idle-window and instant-revocation model are untouched.

I also created **#205** to wire the same flow into the tenant/landlord Expo apps — that's where the real savings land, since tenants are on mobile.

Verify on Windows (only `sharp` expected):

```
npx tsc -p tsconfig.build.json --noEmit
cd web-admin && npx tsc --noEmit && cd ..
npx jest e164 cascade
```

If green:

```
git add -A && git commit -m "feat(auth): remember-this-device trusted session, passwordless re-auth (#202)" && git push
```

Then deploy `api` **and** `web` (both changed), no migration:

```
git pull
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api web
```

Paste the typecheck output and I'll confirm #202 closed. After that, the WhatsApp cost-optimisation thread is essentially done pending your Meta setup (#204) and the mobile wiring (#205).

The lease parser is production-hardened. What I added:

- **Retry with backoff** on transient failures — 429, 500/502/503, 529 (overloaded), and network/timeout errors now retry (default 2 extra attempts) with exponential backoff + jitter, honouring the `Retry-After` header. A blip no longer fails the whole extraction.
- **Error classification** — instead of a raw status dump, users get actionable messages: bad API key (401/403), rate-limited (429), overloaded (529/503), malformed request (400).
- **Configurable** via `DOCUMENT_AI_TIMEOUT_MS` and `DOCUMENT_AI_MAX_RETRIES`, wired into compose + the env example.
- **6 new tests** covering the pure sanitizers (SA date parsing, number coercion, due-day clamp, end≤start drop) and the provider (tool-use success, 529-then-success retry, 401 no-retry classification, JSON-in-text fallback).

`⚙ Grep` — {"pattern": "issueForUser|linkGoogleUser|async googleCallback|roles:", "path": "C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\development\\PMS0.3\\src\\modules\\auth\\auth.service.ts", "output_mode": "content", "-n": true}
> ↳ result: 123: const session = await this.issueForUser(user); 149: const session = await this.issueForUser(user); 168: async issueForUser(user: User): Promise<{ accessTok…

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-04 15:59

Good — that confirms it's **not** a Google-specific bug. The Google callback resolves roles through the exact same path as OTP (`issueForUser`), in this priority: platform admin → partner → agency membership → no role. So "Forbidden resource" means vee1ster@gmail.com logged in but the token came back **without partner access**, and the page it landed on called an endpoint that requires a role it doesn't have.

Almost certainly: **vee1ster@gmail.com isn't actually registered as a partner member yet** (the "Grant login" step wasn't completed, or the partner is still *pending*). Without a `partner_members` row, the login falls through to whatever membership exists — or none — and lands somewhere it isn't allowed.

Fix it as a platform admin at `app.locare.co.za`:

1. **Partners** → find (or **Add**) the partner → if it shows *pending*, click **Activate**.
2. On that row click **Grant login** → enter `vee1ster@gmail.com` → save.
3. Have vee1ster **sign out** (important — this clears the remembered-device token so the stale, role-less session doesn't auto-resume), then log in again with Google.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-05 14:02

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-05 14:03

The move to `/no-access` tells me the earlier SQL didn't actually leave a `partner_members` row attached to the user your **Google** login resolves to — most likely the membership landed on a different/duplicate user row, or the previous `ON CONFLICT (email)` insert didn't take. Google login keys off `google_sub`, so the link has to be on *that* user row.

Here's a robust fix that ignores casing and links the membership to the exact row Google logs you in as. Run it on the VPS:

```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 <<'SQL'
DO $$
DECLARE uid uuid; pid uuid;
BEGIN
  -- the user row Google actually signs in as (prefer the google-linked one)
  SELECT id INTO uid FROM users
   WHERE lower(email)=lower('vee1ster@gmail.com')
   ORDER BY (google_sub IS NOT NULL) DESC, created_at ASC
   LIMIT 1;
  IF uid IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'No user row for that email'; END IF;

  SELECT id INTO pid FROM partners WHERE ref_code='VEE';
  IF pid IS NULL THEN
    INSERT INTO partners (name, contact_email, ref_code, status, commission_rate, banking)
    VALUES ('Vee','vee1ster@gmail.com','VEE','active',0.10,'{}') RETURNING id INTO pid;
  ELSE
    UPDATE partners SET status='active' WHERE id=pid;
  END IF;

  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM partner_members WHERE user_id=uid AND partner_id=pid) THEN
    INSERT INTO partner_members (partner_id, user_id, role) VALUES (pid, uid, 'partner_owner');
  END IF;

  RAISE NOTICE 'linked user % to partner %', uid, pid;
END $$;
SQL
```

Then this diagnostic — it shows every user row for that email, whether each is Google-linked, and its partner membership:

```bash

  psql -U pms -d pms -c "SELECT u.id, u.email, (u.google_sub IS NOT NULL) AS has_google, m.partner_id, p.name, p.status FROM users u LEFT JOIN partner_members m ON m.user_id=u.id LEFT JOIN partners p ON p.id=m.partner_id WHERE lower(u.email)=lower('vee1ster@gmail.com');"
```

You want to see the row where **has_google = t** also showing a **partner_id** and **status = active**. Then have vee1ster **sign out and log in again** with Google.

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-05 14:23

The design is in `docs/LOCARE_PARTNER_KYC_DESIGN.md` and I've broken it into 7 tasks (#206–#212).

The shape of it: a prospective partner **applies** at a public page (individual or business), submits identity/business details + banking, and uploads the required documents (ID/proof of address/bank confirmation for individuals; CIPC registration, director IDs, VAT cert for businesses). That creates a **pending application** — nothing is provisioned yet. A platform admin sees a **review queue** in Admin → Partners → Applications, opens each one to see the fields, masked banking, and documents, then **Approves** (which auto-creates the active partner + grants login), **Rejects** with a reason, or **requests more info**.

Compliance is baked in: PII (ID numbers, banking) encrypted at rest, documents in private storage, consent captured, and every decision audited with reviewer + timestamp + reason — which matters for FICA/POPIA. It's built **provider-ready** via a `KycProvider` interface, so an automated identity/CIPC/sanctions check can slot in later with no schema change.

Two open questions in the doc worth your call before I build:

1. **Commission rate** — set by the admin at approval time (default 10%), or negotiated off-platform and just recorded? I've assumed admin-sets-on-approve.
2. **Document retention for rejected applicants** — POPIA wants a defined window; I've proposed auto-purging documents 90 days after rejection.

Want me to start building **Phase 1 (#206 migration + entities, then #207/#208 backend)**? That's the substantive part and it's all buildable now — the public form and admin UI (#210/#211) come after. Or adjust the two open questions first.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-08-05 17:39

Im still not sure on the login flow of the app. explain it to me

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-05 17:40

Here's the whole picture, start to finish.

**One passwordless system, three front doors.** The web back-office (`app.locare.co.za`), the tenant app, and the landlord app all authenticate against the same API. There are no passwords anywhere — identity is proven by a one-time code (or Google), and the server hands back a signed session token (JWT).

**Step 1 — prove who you are.** On the login screen you enter *either* an email or a mobile number, and the server sends a 6-digit OTP. Delivery goes through the **channel cascade**: WhatsApp first, email as fallback. Right now WhatsApp is off (pending your Meta setup), so it's effectively email-only until then. On the web back-office there's also **Continue with Google**, which skips the code entirely — Google vouches for the email and the server issues the session directly. Either way, you end up in the same place.

**Step 2 — the server decides what you are.** This is the important part. When it issues your token, it resolves your role in a fixed priority order (the `issueForUser` logic):

1. **Platform admin** — if your email is in the `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS` allowlist. (This wins over everything.)
2. **Partner** — if your user is linked in `partner_members` (this is what vee1ster needed).
3. **Agency membership** — if you're a staff member, owner, or tenant of an agency. A *pending* tenant (approved applicant who hasn't signed their lease yet) is blocked here with "sign your lease first."
4. **Nothing** — no matching role → you land on the "You're signed in but not linked yet" page.

The token carries your role(s) plus, depending on type, a `vendorId` (which agency) or `partnerId` (which partner).

**Step 3 — you get routed by role.** The app reads the role from the token and sends you to the right home:

- platform admin → `/admin` (Agencies, Partners, Applications, Billing)
- partner → `/partner` (dashboard, pipeline, commissions)
- owner → `/portal`
- agency staff → `/` (the back office)
- no role → `/no-access`

**Staying signed in.** The token has a short **idle window** (default 10 min) and a session id (`jti`) tracked in Redis. As you use the app it silently refreshes (sliding the window); if you go idle past the window it expires; and signing out (or an admin revoking) kills the Redis entry so the token dies on the very next request — instant revocation, not "valid until expiry."

**Skipping the code next time.** If you tick **"Remember this device"** at login, the server also hands back a long-lived device token (30 days). Next time the app opens, it silently exchanges that for a fresh session — no OTP sent, no cost. Signing out clears it. This is the piece that keeps returning tenants from triggering a WhatsApp/SMS charge on every visit.

So the mental model is: **enter email/phone (or Google) → get verified → server figures out your role → routed to your portal → session stays alive on activity, dies on sign-out, and a trusted device skips the code.**

Anything specific you want me to go deeper on — the role resolution, the OTP delivery, how a tenant gets provisioned, or the token/session mechanics?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-05 18:04

"As it stands" splits into two questions: **who is authorized** (has a role), and **who can actually receive a login** right now. Both matter.

**Who's authorized (has a role):**

- **Platform admins** — whatever emails are in `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS` on the server (that's how you and vernon@ get the admin portal).
- **Partners** — anyone linked in `partner_members`. Right now that's `vee1ster@gmail.com` (once the fixes landed).
- **Agency staff / owners** — members of an agency (Dantalan) with a `vendor_owner`, `property_manager`, or `owner` role.
- **Active tenants** — tenants whose lease is signed (membership is `active`).

**Who's blocked:**

- **Pending tenants** — approved applicants who haven't signed their lease yet get "sign your lease first."
- **Anyone with no membership** — lands on the "signed in but not linked" page. They can authenticate, but there's nothing for them to see.

**The practical constraint right now:** to log in you have to actually receive the code. Two channels:

- **Google** (web back-office only) is working — so any authorized person with a Gmail can sign in at `app.locare.co.za` today. That's the reliable path.
- **Email/phone OTP** depends on outbound email, which rides your HostAfrica SMTP — and that's still gated on the DNS/mail records finishing (#193). Until that's confirmed live, email codes may not be arriving. **WhatsApp** is off until the Meta setup. The **mobile apps have no Google button**, so tenants/landlords rely entirely on OTP delivery — meaning until email (or WhatsApp) is confirmed working, mobile login is effectively blocked.

So the honest summary: **on the web, any authorized account with Google can log in now; email/SMS-based login (and therefore most mobile login) is waiting on the email DNS to finish and/or WhatsApp to be switched on.**

I can't see the live database from here, but if you want the exact list of who actually has access, run this on the VPS and I'll interpret it:

```bash
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T api printenv PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml exec -T postgres \
  psql -U pms -d pms -c "SELECT u.email, 'partner' AS access, p.status FROM partner_members m JOIN users u ON u.id=m.user_id JOIN partners p ON p.id=m.partner_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT u.email, mem.role, mem.status FROM memberships mem JOIN users u ON u.id=mem.user_id ORDER BY 2;"
```

That prints the admin allowlist plus every partner and agency membership with its role and status — the full "who can log in" picture.

### 🧑 Arthur · 2026-08-06 06:48

How do I authorize google accounts?

### 🤖 Claude · 2026-08-06 06:48

There's a subtlety here: the app has **no separate "Google allowlist."** Google login only *verifies* that someone owns an email address — it doesn't grant access by itself. Access comes entirely from that **email having a role** in the system. So "authorizing a Google account" is really just "give that email a role," and it's identical whether they later sign in via Google or via an emailed code.

So to authorize a Google account, you assign its email one of these:

**Platform admin** — add the email to the `PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS` list in `deploy/.env.prod` (comma-separated), then redeploy:

```
# in deploy/.env.prod
PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS=you@gmail.com,vernon@zaaka.io,another@gmail.com
```
```
docker compose --env-file deploy/.env.prod -f deploy/compose.prod.yml up -d --build api
```

They get the admin portal on their next sign-in.

**Partner** — either Admin → Partners → **Grant login** with that email, or approve their KYC/KYB application (which provisions the partner + login automatically).

**Agency staff / owner / tenant** — added through the relevant flow (staff/owner membership, or the tenant add/lease-signing flow). Same idea: the email gets a membership row, and Google login then resolves to it.

The one rule to remember: **the role is baked into the token at login**, so after you authorize an email, that person must **sign out and sign in again** to pick it up.

**One Google-side caveat.** In Google Cloud, your OAuth consent screen is either in **Testing** or **Production** mode:

- **Testing** — only the specific Google accounts you've added as *test users* in Google Cloud can complete "Continue with Google" at all (they'll get an error otherwise). You add them under APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen → Test users.
- **Production** (published) — any Google account can authenticate, and access is then gated purely by whether their email has a role (unknown emails just land on `/no-access`).

Since vee1ster could already sign in with Google, you're likely fine — but if you add someone new and they get a Google *"app hasn't been verified / access denied"* error before even reaching your app, that's the Testing-mode restriction, and the fix is to either add them as a test user or publish the consent screen to Production.

So: **to authorize a Google account, give its email a role in the app (admin/partner/staff/tenant) — and make sure your Google OAuth screen is published (or the person is a listed test user) so they can reach the app in the first place.**
